proposals.name: Complete legible press release document, not an extraction artifact
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the item is a usable, self-contained press release body, judging only the document's integrity and never the interest of its subject. 10 = a complete release: it opens on a subject, develops it, and every sentence is legible prose belonging to that release. 5 = a real release that is truncated mid-sentence, or padded with navigation and share-widget clutter, but still contains a substantial intact body. 2 = a page that is plainly something else (a product catalogue page, a report foreword) yet still reads as continuous prose. 0 = there is no release here at all: the text is a scraper's own meta-commentary about what it failed to find, a stray closing brace or JSON/markdown fragment, or prose so damaged by encoding corruption (apostrophes swallowed into 'Iam', 'weare', runs of 'aA') that sentences cannot be read reliably.
proposals.rationale: R20, R23 and R24 contain no press release whatsoever -- each is a leftover quote-mark and brace followed by the extractor's note that the page held nothing -- and yet the scorecard puts them at card_pct 0.597, 0.724 and 0.713 while the dense model puts them at 0.212, 0.348 and 0.324. R21 (dense 0.249 / card 0.945, the widest over-credit in the slice) is a real post whose every apostrophe has been destroyed, and R32 (0.410 / 0.918) is glyph-damaged the same way. A bank of substantive quality criteria has no slot for 'there is nothing here to read', so topic-shaped criteria keep awarding partial credit; anyone reading the raw bytes sees the failure in one glance.

proposals.name: Announced thing already in force, not merely intended
proposals.instruction: Score the present status of the thing being announced. 10 = it is already effective, shipped, submitted or downloadable as of this text -- a specification whose design files can be downloaded now, a rating that applies to vehicles starting today, a document already submitted to a regulator, hardware already in production and purchasable, an over-the-air update already reaching owners this week. 5 = a firm commitment attached to a specific near-term date on which it takes effect. 0 = everything described is intention, principle or process: 'we commit to', 'hubs are expected to launch later in the year', 'we are developing guiding principles', 'getting this up and running will take us some time', 'details to follow'. Score status only, not how consequential the thing would be if it happened.
proposals.rationale: The dense/scorecard gap tracks this closely in both directions. R06 (dense 0.857 / card 0.123) states the connector design is open today with files available for download; R19 (0.737 / 0.355) says 'starting today, all North American Model S Long Range Plus vehicles have an official EPA-rated range of 402 miles'; R35 (0.956 / 0.338) says the hardware is already in production and buyable today. Against these, R05 (0.164 / 0.669) offers hubs 'expected to launch later in the year', R34 (0.130 / 0.676) is a list of commitments with no instrument, and R37 (0.594 / 1.000, the scorecard's maximum in the slice) says only that a redesign 'will take us some time'. A rubric can credit an intention's ambition as easily as an action's effect; a reader cannot.

proposals.name: First disclosure here, not restatement of already-public facts
proposals.instruction: Score whether the central fact appears to be entering the public record with this document. 10 = the core claim is disclosed here, with no indication the audience already knows it and no dependence on a prior announcement to make sense. 5 = a genuinely new increment attached to a substantial recap of prior announcements. 0 = the text openly concedes the news is old -- 'as you have likely heard by now', 'in August 2020 we announced a temporary ban ... today we are officially codifying it', 'last month our CEO announced X ... today we're announcing three steps forward' -- or the body is essentially a chronology of initiatives launched in previous years. Judge only novelty of disclosure within the text, not importance.
proposals.rationale: R12 (dense 0.478 / card 0.887) is explicit that the ban it announces has been in force since August 2020 and is merely being 'codified'. R13, R41 and R58 (dense 0.317, 0.299, 0.299 against card 0.737, 0.773, 0.773) all open by telling the reader 'as you have likely heard by now'. R28 (0.515 / 0.915) frames itself as follow-through on last month's announcement. Completeness- and context-shaped criteria positively reward this recap structure, because a restatement is by construction well-supported and well-contextualised.

proposals.name: Specified, unresolved conflict with a named external institution
proposals.instruction: Score the presence and specificity of live conflict with an outside body. 10 = the release engages a named external institution -- a regulator, a court, a law-enforcement agency, a broadcaster, a newspaper, a petitioner -- in an unresolved dispute, and lays out who, what is alleged, and what step is being taken next. 5 = an outside body is named but the posture is cooperative or the matter is closed. 0 = no external party stands in tension with the issuer; third parties appear only as partners being praised or as sources being cited approvingly.
proposals.rationale: The four sharpest dense-high items in the slice are all of this shape: R07 (dense 0.986 / card 0.447) on a state agency's intended lawsuit, R49 (0.935 / 0.573) on an NHTSA petition brought by a short-seller, R48 (0.850 / 0.270) on reporters arrested at a factory, R43 (0.761 / 0.399) on a libel action filed against a broadcaster. Meanwhile the partner-praise items R27 (0.584 / 0.048) and R45 (0.314 / 0.672) name outside organisations only to compliment them. Most rubric vocabularies for corporate communications are built around clarity, support and tone; an adversarial release scores badly on tone precisely when it is most reportable.

proposals.name: Informs a general public rather than reassuring affected customers
proposals.instruction: Score who the text is built for. 10 = a third-person account of what happened, addressed to any reader, whose content is the facts rather than what the reader should do or feel. 5 = a signed first-person message that nonetheless carries hard, generally-relevant facts. 0 = a second-person crisis or community letter to the directly affected ('Dear Target Guest', 'Dear Host'), dominated by apology, reassurance and recipient instructions -- 'we take this crime seriously', 'you can shop with confidence', 'you will not be responsible for fraudulent charges', 'please check the FAQ page' -- so that the informational payload is service advice for one constituency.
proposals.rationale: This is the single most consistently over-credited shape in the slice. R13, R41 and R58 (dense ~0.30 against card 0.74-0.77) are the same customer letter three times; R02 (0.263 / 0.826) is a long letter to hosts; R10 (0.058 / 0.536) reformats one regional event; R08 (0.283 / 0.751) is a values foreword to a report. Reassurance letters are unusually strong on the qualities a rubric can name -- clear structure, plain language, empathy, explicit next steps, named signatory -- and unusually weak as a source of anything to write up.

proposals.name: Quotations carry information rather than ceremonial praise
proposals.instruction: Score the informational load of quoted material. 10 = the quotes are load-bearing -- they commit to something, contest something, concede something, or state a fact the body does not otherwise contain -- OR the release carries no quotes at all and is fact-dense throughout. 5 = one informative quote among several decorative ones. 0 = every quote is interchangeable executive enthusiasm ('mobile is, without question, the channel of the future', 'we are thrilled to welcome', 'the potential for this business is virtually unlimited') that could be deleted with no factual loss. Explicitly do not reward quote count or quote length.
proposals.rationale: R27 (dense 0.584 / card 0.048) is three consecutive paragraphs of quoted vision containing no number, date or commitment, and the scorecard buries it; R45 (0.314 / 0.672) is mostly mutual executive praise, and the scorecard lifts it. In the other direction the quote-free items are exactly where the dense model runs far ahead: R31 (0.942 / 0.249), R49 (0.935 / 0.573), R06 (0.857 / 0.123), R55 (0.799 / 0.352). A criterion that asks whether a release 'includes supporting quotations from named executives' rewards the wrong half of that pattern twice over.

proposals.name: Auditable present measurement versus sponsored multi-year projection
proposals.instruction: Score the provenance and time horizon of the load-bearing numbers together. 10 = the numbers measure something that has already happened by a method the reader could check or reproduce -- a named published index series with stated coverage and history, a regulatory filing, a stated dollar commitment with a payment schedule. 5 = the issuer's own operational data, but disclosed with definitions, periods and comparison bases. 0 = the numbers are forecasts years out, or come from a study the subject commissioned about itself, presented as findings: '9.3 million new jobs and $1.6 trillion by 2026', 'demand will grow at least 30 times by 2040', 'could jump more than 80% over the next six months'. Large magnitude must not raise the score; checkability and pastness must.
proposals.rationale: R09 (dense 0.235 / card 0.594) carries the biggest numbers in the slice and they are an analyst forecast commissioned by their own subject; R42 (0.113 / 0.587) and R29 (0.140 / 0.635) are outlook pieces built on projected barrels and megawatts. Against these, R31, R53 and R57 (dense 0.942, 0.915, 0.932 against card 0.249, 0.205, 0.242) contain nothing but a named index's measured monthly series with 27 years of published history. Any criterion of the form 'claims are supported by data' cannot separate a measured series from a sponsored projection, and this slice shows the scorecard inverting the two.

proposals.name: Superlative benchmarked against named comparators and stated measurement standard
proposals.instruction: Score superlative claims by how checkable they are made. 10 = first/fastest/largest/longest is asserted against specific named rivals or a named measurement standard, with the metric identified and the qualifications stated -- 0-60 mph against the LaFerrari and the Porsche 918, range on the EPA cycle versus the NEDC cycle, ranked cities with year-over-year percentages, ratings from a named safety regulator, an asterisked note on test conditions. 5 = a superlative with a number attached but no comparator or standard. 0 = self-applied labels with nothing behind them: 'global leader', 'the world's #1', 'our biggest ever', 'the most important innovations in our history'. Score the benchmarking, not whether the claim is impressive.
proposals.rationale: R03 (dense 0.741 / card 0.031) and R17 (0.778 / 0.382) are the same text, benchmarked in every sentence against named rival cars and two named range cycles, with a footnote on test method; R19 (0.737 / 0.355) quantifies a nearly 20% gain against a named prior model year; R53 and R57 rank named cities with percentages. Against these, R09 (0.235 / 0.594) and R32 (0.410 / 0.918) lead with unbenchmarked leadership language. A rubric can credit 'makes a strong claim of distinction' without ever asking against what.

proposals.name: Concretely enumerated scale of people, sites or units affected
proposals.instruction: Score the stated size of what changes, in checkable units. 10 = a large affected set is enumerated -- 340,000 team members and $200 million over four years, twelve stores this week plus more than 1,000 remodels and the last remaining state in the country, every vehicle produced from today onward. 5 = a real but modest footprint, enumerated. 0 = a single site, a single local occasion, or a single procedural step: one childcare centre for 116 children, one regional conference moved online, one flight's arrivals at one airport, a proposed briefing schedule in one case. Count only scale that the text actually states; ignore implied or rhetorical scale.
proposals.rationale: R15 (dense 0.488 / card 0.147) and R18 (0.884 / 0.457) enumerate large footprints and the scorecard under-rates both. At the other end R47 (0.109 / 0.928), R10 (0.058 / 0.536), R30 (0.007 / 0.659) and R22 (0.106 / 0.686) are each one building, one event, one flight or one docket step, and the scorecard rates all four in its upper half. R30 is the lowest dense percentile in the whole slice at 0.007 while the scorecard has it at 0.659 -- a well-written small thing.

proposals.name: Changes options for competitors, regulators or an entire market
proposals.instruction: Score how far the consequences reach past the issuer's own customers. 10 = the action alters what other organisations can or must do -- a proprietary interface released as an open standard with specification files published and standards bodies engaged, a platform made available to third-party institutions to build on, a step that subjects the issuer to a new external supervisory regime. 5 = binding consequences for a named partner or a defined slice of an industry. 0 = wholly self-contained: the issuer's own values, its own emissions, its own employee perks, its own community programme, with no other organisation's choices touched.
proposals.rationale: R06 (dense 0.857 / card 0.123) hands a connector design to every charging operator and vehicle manufacturer in North America and asks standards bodies to codify it; R27 (0.584 / 0.048) offers an interoperable platform to third-party financial institutions; R55 (0.799 / 0.352) starts a process that will place the issuer under public-market obligations. All three are near the bottom of the scorecard. Against them R08 (0.283 / 0.751), R32 (0.410 / 0.918) and R47 (0.109 / 0.928) are entirely inward-facing and all sit in the scorecard's top third. Rubrics tend to ask what the issuer did, not whom else it binds.

proposals.name: A named person acts, not merely endorses
proposals.instruction: Score whether the item has a protagonist. 10 = a specific identifiable individual does something inside the text -- promotes named executives and says what each of them built, personally hosts guests in a space he made, is struck by a vehicle and sustains described injuries, is arrested, files an action -- so the item has a scene and an actor. 5 = a named individual writes in the first person with content that only that person could have written. 0 = an undifferentiated corporate 'we' or 'the team' throughout, with individuals appearing only inside approving quotation marks or as a signature.
proposals.rationale: R25 and R39 (both dense 0.906 against card 0.341 and 0.345) are one executive's own email naming five people and describing what each of them did; R38 (0.631 / 0.113) puts a named public figure in a room he built and offers dates to meet him; R48 (0.850 / 0.270) has named roles, measured lacerations and an arrest on felony counts. Against these, R34 (0.130 / 0.676) and R36 (0.276 / 0.642) are authorless institutional prose that the scorecard rates well above them. A rubric asks whether people are quoted; it does not ask whether anyone acts.

proposals.name: Discloses something adverse or costly to the issuer
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the content runs against the issuer's own interest. 10 = the text puts on the record, in specific terms, something the issuer would rather not publish -- an agency's allegation of systematic misconduct reproduced in detail, a petition alleging a dangerous product defect, revised quarterly guidance moved downward with the new figures, employees hurt, a cost the issuer must bear. 5 = an adverse matter is acknowledged but only in general terms. 0 = uniformly favourable content, or a rebuttal in which nothing at all is conceded and the entire point is that no defect, no investigation and no wrongdoing exist.
proposals.rationale: R07 (dense 0.986 / card 0.447) reproduces the discrimination allegation it is fighting; R49 (0.935 / 0.573) names the petition against it and the alleged failure mode. The contrast inside the same genre is what makes this a distinct criterion rather than a restatement of conflict: R11 (0.403 / 0.765) and R14 (0.382 / 0.874) are equally combative rebuttals in which the disclosed content is wholly exculpatory -- 'there is no safety defect', 'NHTSA has not opened any investigation', 'nobody has brought a claim' -- and the dense model puts both far below R07 and R49 while the scorecard puts them far above. Concession, not combat, is what carries.

proposals.name: Facts per word; lede available in opening sentences
proposals.instruction: Score informational density rather than length or thoroughness. 10 = an accurate opening paragraph could be written from the first two sentences, and nearly every subsequent paragraph adds a distinct checkable fact; very short items score high when they are dense. 5 = real facts, reached only after several paragraphs of mission, context or gratitude. 0 = long, with substance thinly spread through narrative, values, thanks and repeated 'key takeaways' blocks, so that screens at a time can be cut with no factual loss. Explicitly penalise repetition of the same takeaway in more than one place, and do not reward word count.
proposals.rationale: R55 (dense 0.799 / card 0.352) is a single paragraph naming exactly what was submitted, to whom, and under which rule; R49 (0.935 / 0.573) and R31 (0.942 / 0.249) are similarly compressed and similarly under-rated. Against them the scorecard's favourites are its longest items: R02 (0.263 / 0.826), R08 (0.283 / 0.751), R56 (0.229 / 0.717), R21 (0.249 / 0.945), and R12 and R36, both of which print their key-takeaway block twice. Any bank that credits thoroughness, structure and completeness will systematically pay for length, which is the clearest single artefact visible in this slice.

proposals.name: Distinctive quotable voice rather than interchangeable corporate template
proposals.instruction: Score the register of the writing itself. 10 = an unmistakable authorial voice a reporter would quote verbatim for its manner -- sustained satire, an abrupt one-word sign-off, unhedged internal candour, jokes that land -- copy that no other organisation's communications function could have produced. 5 = competent house style with a few lines that stand out. 0 = fully templated: dateline, ticker, benefit-laden subheads, 'About [Company]' block, and not one sentence anyone would reproduce for how it is written. Judge only manner of expression; a release with no facts at all can still score 10 here, and a fact-rich release can score 0.
proposals.rationale: R01 (dense 0.686 / card 0.348) is a wholly satirical product announcement containing essentially no verifiable fact -- every substance-shaped criterion must mark it down, while a reader recognises copy that writes itself up. R25 and R39 (0.906 / ~0.34) carry lines like 'that is insanely badass' inside an otherwise routine personnel announcement, and R06 (0.857 / 0.123) closes a standards release with the single word 'Enjoy.' The scorecard has no way to register voice as evidence of anything, so it reads all three as thin.

proposals.name: Formal filing or legally consequential step by the issuer
proposals.instruction: Score whether the item is, or reports, an act by the issuer that has legal force. 10 = a registration statement submitted to a securities regulator under a cited rule, an action filed in court, meeting machinery that carries legal effect (record dates, control numbers, legal proxies, a stated password and deadline), a specification lodged with standards bodies. 5 = a policy that binds the issuer's users with stated enforcement consequences and effective dates. 0 = communication with no legal standing at all: a blog post, a marketing announcement, an aspiration with no instrument behind it. Judge legal consequence, not the readability of the legal language.
proposals.rationale: R55 (dense 0.799 / card 0.352) is nothing but a Rule 135 notice and disclaimer, and the scorecard reads it as thin boilerplate; R51 (0.792 / 0.311) is pure procedural machinery -- control numbers, legal proxies, a submission deadline; R43 (0.761 / 0.399) opens on a filed libel action. Criteria for prose quality, engagement and accessibility treat statutory language as bad writing, which exactly inverts its significance: the more constrained the language, the more binding the act it records.

proposals.name: Paid-newswire dateline, ticker and legal-trailer formalism
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH of the paid-wire distribution formatting kit is visibly present in the text. Count only visible elements: (a) a capitalised city dateline followed by a date and a dash, e.g. 'SAN FRANCISCO -- September 20, 2021 --' or 'MINNEAPOLIS - January 10, 2014'; (b) an explicit wire-service marker such as '/PRNewswire/'; (c) a stock-exchange ticker in parentheses attached to the organisation's name, e.g. '(NYSE: CRM)', '(NASDAQ: CTSH)', '(LSE: MONI)'; (d) a stacked headline-plus-subhead deck sitting above the dateline; (e) the set phrase 'today announced' / 'today unveiled'; (f) a closing 'About <organisation>' block or a securities / forward-looking / Rule-135 legal paragraph. 0 = none of these elements present; 3 = one element; 5 = two or three; 8 = four or five; 10 = essentially the whole kit. Score presence and prominence of the FORMATTING ONLY. You must NOT judge whether this formatting is good, professional, clear, or appropriate, and you must not consider whether the announcement itself is important.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4. The wire kit is a purchasing and vendor decision taken before a word is drafted, so it is a fingerprint of budget and agency habit, not of whether a journalist would write the item up. R52 carries the entire kit (headline + subhead deck + 'Oct 4, 2012 TEANECK, N.J. and LONDON, Oct. 4, 2012 / PRNewswire / --' + '(NASDAQ: CTSH)' + '(LSE: MONI)' + 'About Cognizant'); R30 carries it in the Salesforce house form ('SAN FRANCISCO -- September 20, 2021 -- Salesforce (NYSE: CRM) ... today announced'); R41 and R57 carry the Target form ('MINNEAPOLIS - October 19, 2017', 'MINNEAPOLIS - January 10, 2014', '(NYSE: TGT)'); R03, R05 and R07 carry the S&P DJI form ('NEW YORK, June 29, 2021:'). By contrast R04, R31, R20 and R46 carry none of it while describing substantively comparable events. Tagged mixed because organisations tend to buy wire distribution for the announcements they themselves treat as material, so the same upstream choice can co-vary with genuine news value.
proposals.upstream_parent: distribution tier the item went out on (a paid newswire and/or outside PR-agency house style) versus the organisation's own newsroom page

proposals.name: Owned-newsroom page furniture and CMS template residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH content-management-system and web-page furniture from the hosting newsroom page has survived into the text, as distinct from the body of the release. Count: (a) a byline/date/category slug line in template form, e.g. 'By Airbnb * May 3, 2023 - Company, Destinations' or 'By Margaret Richardson * December 5, 2019 * Community'; (b) social share-button text such as 'Share Share on Facebook Tweet Share on Twitter Share Share on LinkedIn Pin It Share on Pinterest'; (c) section-tag strings such as 'Article reads in team', 'Article reads in lifestyle', 'Read more about: Listicle', or a bare 'Author  Theme' header; (d) subscription or registration prompts such as 'Sign up to receive updates via email' or 'Not registered? Receive daily email alerts'; (e) a boilerplate 'About <organisation>' paragraph appended after the body; (f) a summary block (for example a 'Key Takeaways' list) that is reproduced twice verbatim, one after the other. 0 = no such furniture, the text is pure release body; 10 = furniture is abundant and interleaved throughout. Score only how much furniture is visible. You must NOT judge whether the furniture is helpful, tidy, or good, and must not let it colour your view of the release itself.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4 companion / MODE 1. The furniture is emitted by the template of whichever site hosted the item and is invariant to what the release says. R13 carries the full share-widget strip plus 'Article reads in team'; R58 carries 'Article reads in lifestyle'; R42 ends in the 'About Airbnb was born in 2007...' boilerplate plus 'Read more about: Listicle'; R50 opens with a bare 'Author     Theme  Metals' header; R36 carries the subscription interrupt 'Not registered? Receive daily email alerts, subscriber notes & personalize your experience.' mid-body; R03, R05 and R07 all carry 'Sign up to receive updates via email'; R23, R25, R43 and R45 each repeat their whole 'Key Takeaways' block twice verbatim, which is a template duplication artefact rather than authorial repetition. R04, R31 and R59 carry none of it. Purely a venue/plumbing trace, so not mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: the publishing venue and the CMS template of the page the item was captured from (which newsroom platform hosted it), plus the harvesting of that page

proposals.name: Capture integrity: extraction residue and mid-sentence truncation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the text shows signs of being an incomplete or failed page capture rather than a whole self-contained document. Count: (a) stray serialisation characters with no textual role, such as a lone double-quote on its own line, a closing brace '}', or a triple-backtick fence; (b) meta-commentary that describes the page instead of being the page, e.g. sentences beginning 'The provided raw page content does not appear to contain a press release' or 'This page does not appear to contain a press release'; (c) a body that stops mid-sentence or mid-word with no closing; (d) an absent headline, dateline or opening so that the text begins abruptly in the middle of an argument; (e) collapsed whitespace runs or glued-together words where layout was lost. 0 = a clean, complete, self-contained document; 5 = the document is intact but visibly clipped at one end; 10 = the text is mostly capture residue with little or no release content in it. Score only the extent of capture damage. You must NOT judge whether the surviving content is good, and must not reward or penalise the item for what the damage hides.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. R14, R29 and R33 are the extreme case: each consists of a dangling double-quote, a '}' and a code fence, followed by a note that the page contained no press release at all - i.e. the entire item is pipeline residue. Milder truncation is widespread and equally upstream: R13 stops mid-word at 'While this educati', R01 stops at 'a ban on party ho', R23 at 'Airbnb listings were “wishli', R44 and R56 stop mid-paragraph, R52 at 'combines a passion for client s'. R31 and R47 are the same Tesla body with and without its headline line, differing only in what the capture retained. Nothing here is about the release, so not mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: the corpus scraping and extraction pipeline interacting with the structure of the source page (a corpus-construction artefact, not a property of the release)

proposals.name: Character-encoding corruption (mojibake) density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH visible character-encoding corruption is present in the text. Count occurrences of: (a) apostrophes, em-dashes or curly quotes mis-rendered as a stray letter 'a' glued inside or between words, e.g. 'Itas', 'thatas', 'worldas', 'Salesforceas', 'Iam', 'Weave' (for 'we have'), 'salariesafor', 'basisamaking', 'community a our Ohana'; (b) runs of isolated capital 'A' characters standing where non-breaking spaces or bullets were, e.g. 'A A A A A'; (c) replacement boxes, question marks or stray '?' where punctuation should be, e.g. a trailing '?' in a headline; (d) sentences that break off at a dropped character, e.g. 'reach out to us at  ' with nothing following. Score 0 if the text is clean throughout; 3 if there are a handful of instances; 7 if corruption appears in most paragraphs; 10 if it is pervasive and affects reading on nearly every line. Score only how much corruption is visible. You must NOT judge whether the writing is good, and must NOT treat corruption as evidence about the care, competence or importance of the item.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. The corruption is deterministic given the source platform and the scrape, and is invisible in the document as its authors wrote it. R08 is saturated ('Itas a challenge', 'thatas just what', 'Weave completed', 'salariesafor both men and women'); R18 likewise ('the worldas #1 CRM provider', 'Salesforceas commitment', 'Iam proud to share'); R44 combines both forms ('Iam helping develop Salesforceas plan') with long 'A A A A' runs; R60 has 'our community a our Ohana' and 'forthright a which is exactly'; R13 carries a stray '?' in its headline. R41, R57, R59 and R48 are clean. Because the parent is a decoding step and nothing else, this is a pure nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: the character encoding of the source page and the decoding step of the harvesting pipeline - which in practice tags which organisation's CMS the item was pulled from

proposals.name: Third-party trade-press or analyst copy rather than first-party release
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the text reads as an article written ABOUT an organisation by an outside reporter or analyst, rather than as a statement issued BY an organisation. Positive indicators: the organisation is referred to only in the third person with a legal suffix ('Murray Energy Corp.', 'Ryanair', 'Volkswagen AG') and never as 'we' or 'our'; multiple outside sources are introduced with 'according to' or 'said' and identified by employer and job title; forecasts and figures are attributed to a named research house or agency; the piece carries standalone reported-news subheads set on their own lines; the piece contains no call to action, no product promotion and no institutional first-person voice. Negative indicators (push the score down): first-person plural referring to the issuing organisation, a company dateline, a call to action, or a sign-off by an executive of the organisation. 0 = unambiguously a first-party statement in the organisation's own voice; 10 = unambiguously outside reportage or analyst commentary. Score only the voice and provenance signature. You must NOT judge whether the writing is good, accurate or interesting.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. R02 is a legal-docket write-up in pure reportage voice ('The U.S. Mine Safety and Health Administration and the plaintiffs told the U.S. District Court ... in a joint filing Dec. 19'); R28 is a trade-magazine story with its own subheads 'Unchecked Passports' and 'Airport Security Lapse' and quoted spokespeople from three different organisations; R36 is Platts Analytics commodity analysis with 'according to estimates by Platts Analytics' and a quoted head of refining economics; R56 is an S&P Global grid-reliability feature quoting PJM and MISO officials; R50 is an S&P Global Market Intelligence metals feature quoting a senior analyst and a managing director. None of these is a press release at all, so their textual signature is a property of corpus assembly, not of any organisation's communications - hence not mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: which source site the item was harvested from - corpus source-mixing that placed trade-press and analyst articles into a pool nominally of press releases

proposals.name: Encapsulated internal letter or all-hands email republished as a release
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the item is a wrapper around a document that was originally addressed to an internal or customer audience rather than to the press. Count: (a) an explicit framing line that hands off to another document, e.g. 'The following email was just sent to Tesla employees', 'Below is an email Co-founder, CEO and Head of Community Brian Chesky sent to Airbnb hosts today', 'The message below was posted from Target on Dec. 19, 2013'; (b) a salutation addressed to a non-press audience, e.g. 'Dear Target Guest', 'Dear Host'; (c) sustained second-person address to employees, hosts, guests or customers ('thank you for your incredible efforts', 'your patience, understanding and loyalty'); (d) a personal sign-off giving an individual's name and job title at the end, e.g. 'Gregg Steinhafel Chairman, President and CEO, Target', 'Brian C. Cornell Chairman and Chief Executive Officer', 'Cindy Robbins is EVP, Global Employee Success, at Salesforce'. 0 = none of these, the item addresses a general or press readership throughout; 10 = the item is wholly a reproduced letter or email with framing and salutation and sign-off. Score only the extent of the letter/email packaging. You must NOT judge whether the letter is well written, sincere or worth reading.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Who drafted the document and for whom is upstream of the text and leaves this exact packaging trace. R09 and R55 open with 'The following email was just sent to Tesla employees' and never address a reader outside the company; R46 opens 'Below is an email ... sent to Airbnb hosts today ... Dear Host'; R11, R12 and R53 are the identical 'Dear Target Guest' letter with a CEO sign-off and a nested second document ('The message below was posted from Target on Dec. 19, 2013'); R19 is a CSR-report foreword signed 'Brian C. Cornell'; R08 closes with a third-person author note. R17, R35, R41 and R52 have none of it. Tagged mixed honestly: an internal all-hands email that surfaces publicly can be genuinely newsworthy precisely because it was not written for the press, so the parent plausibly causes real news value too.
proposals.upstream_parent: the item's origin in internal or customer communications drafted by a named executive and then republished, rather than in a press office drafting for external distribution

proposals.name: Reactive rebuttal framing that names an external antagonist
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the text is organised as a response to a specific outside actor or outside account, as opposed to a self-initiated announcement. Count: (a) a named external party - a regulator, agency, publication, television programme, petition, blog post, short-seller, court or news outlet - identified in the text; (b) that party's claims restated in order to be contradicted; (c) an enumerated refutation structure ('First ... Second ... Third ... Fourth ...') or a run of paragraphs each opening by correcting a stated allegation; (d) explicit characterisations of the outside account as false, incorrect, misleading, preposterous or spun. 0 = no outside actor is answered anywhere; 5 = an outside actor is named and briefly answered inside a longer item; 10 = the entire item exists to rebut a named outside account point by point. Score only the extent of the rebuttal structure. You must NOT judge who is right, whether the rebuttal is convincing, or whether responding was a good idea.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Whether a release was forced by an outside event is an unseen production fact, but it leaves an unmistakable textual fingerprint. R15 names the California DFEH and answers its intended lawsuit ('A narrative spun by the DFEH and a handful of plaintiff firms'); R16 is titled 'Misfortune' and rebuts a named magazine paragraph by paragraph ('Fortune's article is fundamentally incorrect'); R21 uses the explicit 'First ... Second ... Third ... Fourth' ladder against a blog post and NHTSA reporting; R26 opens 'This petition is completely false and was brought by a Tesla short-seller'; R48 sues and answers a named BBC programme; R51 narrates an incident involving named 'RGJ' employees. R37, R39 and R42 have none of this. Tagged mixed because a genuine external controversy is often independently newsworthy, so the parent can drive real news value as well as this fingerprint.
proposals.upstream_parent: a reactive trigger on the production side - an outside event, filing or press story forced this item to be written at speed, rather than it arriving from a planned announcement calendar

proposals.name: Series back-reference presupposing an earlier announcement
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the text assumes the reader already knows about a previous announcement in the same programme, rather than introducing its subject from scratch. Count: (a) dated callbacks to the organisation's own earlier announcements, e.g. 'In August 2020 we announced a temporary ban on all parties', 'Last month Brian Chesky ... announced a set of safety directives', 'Earlier this year, we launched our Live and Work Anywhere initiative', 'in 2019 we joined the Mayor of London in support of new rules'; (b) continuation vocabulary used as if the programme is already established - 'codifying', 'update', 'continued commitment', 'builds on', 'expands', 'next phase', 'additional locations', 'as part of'; (c) an explicit recap section such as 'How we got here' or 'A quick history lesson'; (d) an editorial revision stamp such as 'This article was updated September 2, 2021'. Push the score DOWN for language that introduces a programme with no prior instalment assumed ('For the first time', 'Introducing', 'today we are opening ... to the world', 'a first-ever analysis'). 0 = fully self-contained, presupposes nothing; 10 = largely unintelligible without the earlier instalment. Score only the extent of presupposition. You must NOT judge whether being early or late in a series is good, and must not judge whether the programme matters.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3. Position in the issuing stream is unobservable, but presupposition is directly visible. R25 is almost entirely back-reference ('In August 2020 we announced a temporary ban ... today we are officially codifying the ban', plus a 'How we got here' recap and a callback to 'our recent Summer Release'); R01 opens 'Last month Brian Chesky ... announced' and calls itself 'part of a continued commitment'; R39 opens 'Earlier this year, we launched our Live and Work Anywhere initiative'; R38 back-references 2019 and 'last year'; R13 carries the stamp 'This article was updated September 2, 2021' and a 'A quick history lesson' section; R17 frames itself as building 'on Target and Apple's more than 15-year relationship'. The opposite pole is visible in R04 ('today we are opening our EV connector design to the world'), R43 ('A first-ever analysis'), R06 ('For the very first time'). Tagged mixed because a genuine first-of-its-kind announcement plausibly IS more newsworthy, so the parent has a real-quality path as well.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the run of releases this organisation has issued on the same programme (a first-of-its-kind announcement versus the nth routine update)

proposals.name: Calendar-slot and scheduled-cadence anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the text is pinned to a recurring calendar slot or a fixed publication cadence, as opposed to standing free of the calendar. Count: (a) reporting-period template language indicating a scheduled data release - 'Data released today for April 2021', a 'YEAR-OVER-YEAR' section head, repeated 'up from ... in the previous month', 'The charts on the following page compare ...'; (b) fiscal-period vocabulary - 'fourth quarter 2013 adjusted EPS', 'as we enter the final few weeks of this quarter', 'Q1 2023', 'annual meeting of stockholders'; (c) seasonal or retail-calendar framing - 'With just a few weeks left until Christmas', 'ahead of a busy summer travel season', 'To start the year on a high', 'this year we're expecting over 300 million guest arrivals'; (d) dated and clock-timed go-live, deadline or embargo instructions - 'beginning February 7 at 10:00 AM PT', 'On Mon., July 15, and Tues., July 16', 'no later than 2:00 PM Pacific Time on September 17, 2020', 'Starting this Sunday, Dec. 11'. 0 = no calendar anchoring at all; 10 = the item is wholly an instance of a scheduled slot, with its structure dictated by the period it reports. Score only the extent of calendar anchoring. You must NOT judge whether the timing is well chosen or whether a scheduled item is worth less than an unscheduled one.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3 (calendar position) with a MODE 4 timing-convention component. R03, R05 and R07 are three instances of one monthly template, sharing near-identical opening sentences, the same 'YEAR-OVER-YEAR' head and the same closing 'The charts on the following page compare ...' line, differing only in the month and the city rankings - the strongest possible cadence fingerprint. R57 is quarter-end guidance ('fourth quarter 2013 adjusted EPS of $1.20 to $1.30'); R09 and R55 open on 'the final few weeks of this quarter'; R24 is proxy-season logistics with clock-timed registration deadlines; R58 is Christmas-week retail timing ('Starting this Sunday, Dec. 11'); R32 sets 'Mon., July 15, and Tues., July 16'; R06 sets 'February 7 at 10:00 AM PT'. R48 and R31 carry none of it. Tagged mixed because release timing is chosen partly in anticipation of news demand, so the parent can also touch genuine pickup value.
proposals.upstream_parent: where the item falls in the issuer's release calendar and the surrounding news cycle (monthly data cadence, quarter-end, earnings and proxy season, holiday retail season) together with the embargo and go-live conventions attached to that slot

proposals.name: Organisation-prominence self-descriptors and own-name saturation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the text asserts the issuing organisation's scale and market standing and saturates itself with its own name and product-brand names. Count: (a) self-positioning epithets attached to the organisation or its product - 'the global leader in CRM', 'the leading measure of U.S. home prices', 'the most proven in North America', 'the Quickest Production Car in the World', 'the longest range production electric vehicle by far', 'a leader in all that we do'; (b) scale statistics about the organisation itself rather than about the news - counts of customers, employees, hosts, listings, stores, guest arrivals, network nodes, dollars invested; (c) an 'About <organisation>' recital of founding story and cumulative totals; (d) repeated use of the organisation's own name and trademarked product names where a generic noun would do, and superscript footnote markers glued to those in-house statistics ('respondents7', 'listings2', 'Host9'). 0 = the organisation is barely named and makes no standing claims; 5 = a few standing claims or in-house statistics; 10 = the text is saturated with self-naming, self-statistics and standing claims. Score only how much of this material is present. You must NOT assess whether the claims are true, justified, proportionate or well written, and must not judge the organisation.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4. Organisation prominence is an unseen upstream factor; its visible trace is self-positioning boilerplate and in-house statistics. R30 opens 'Salesforce (NYSE: CRM), the global leader in CRM' and then reports IDC totals about Salesforce itself; R03, R05 and R07 each call the index 'the leading measure of U.S. home prices' and cite '27 years of history'; R04 calls the connector 'the most proven in North America' and adds 'NACS vehicles outnumber CCS two-to-one'; R31 and R47 stack 'third fastest accelerating production car ever produced' and 'the longest range production electric vehicle by far'; R42 closes with the 'About Airbnb ... 4 million Hosts ... more than 1 billion guest arrivals' recital; R23, R43 and R45 carry dense footnote-marked in-house statistics ('respondents7', 'Host9', 'listings2'). R02, R28 and R49 carry almost none. Tagged mixed because a large, prominent organisation with standing press relationships genuinely does generate items journalists are likelier to write up, so the parent has a real-quality path alongside the nuisance one.
proposals.upstream_parent: the size, prominence and existing media relationships of the issuing organisation (i.e. which organisation is speaking), which is unobservable directly but drives how much self-positioning language the house style carries

proposals.name: Genuine press-release content vs. extraction artifact
proposals.instruction: Score whether the text is actual substantive press-release/news content issued by an organization, versus a failed-extraction placeholder, page-navigation debris, or meta-commentary about a missing document. A 10 = the entire text is coherent, on-topic press-release prose with a clear subject and no artifacts. A 0 = the text is dominated by phrases like 'does not appear to contain a press release,' disclaims finding a body, or is otherwise a non-answer/error message rather than substantive content.
proposals.rationale: Rows R04, R30, and R47 are all failed-extraction messages ('The provided raw page content does not appear to contain a press release...') with essentially no real content, yet all three sit in the dense_low_card_high half of the slice, meaning the scorecard rated this non-content noticeably higher than the dense model did. A scorecard built from criteria that ask about presence of quotes, numbers, or structure can be fooled by boilerplate refusal language into assigning nonzero credit; a dedicated artifact-detection criterion would floor these correctly.

proposals.name: Dated, recurring index/data-drop release
proposals.instruction: Score how much the release reads as a dated, recurring release of a standardized quantitative indicator (e.g., a price index, economic gauge, or benchmark) presented with specific comparative statistics (month-over-month, year-over-year, city/sector rankings) attributed to a named issuing organization. A 10 = the release is centered on a 'today released' report of fresh comparative numbers with named leaders/laggards and historical comparison. A 0 = no dated quantitative release is present, only narrative or promotional prose.
proposals.rationale: R28, R33, and R37 are all S&P Dow Jones Case-Shiller home-price index releases -- terse, numbers-dense, dated 'today released' reports with city-by-city rankings -- and all three sit deep in the dense_high_card_low half, with dense ranking them near the top of the whole pool while the scorecard ranks them near the bottom. This is a clean, three-times-replicated case where a whole genre (scheduled economic-indicator drops) is systematically undervalued by the scorecard relative to dense.

proposals.name: Acute adversarial incident with verifiable procedural facts
proposals.instruction: Score the degree to which the release centers on a discrete adversarial event -- an altercation, arrest, criminal charge, lawsuit, or safety incident -- narrated with verifiable procedural specifics (who was involved, when it happened, what agency responded, what injury or charge resulted). A 10 = a specific, dated adversarial incident is narrated with concrete procedural detail. A 0 = no adversarial incident is described, only routine business activity.
proposals.rationale: R09 (two journalists trespassing at the Gigafactory, a physical altercation, injuries, and a felony arrest), R21 (Tesla suing the BBC's Top Gear for libel), and R34 (a state agency's discrimination lawsuit against Tesla) are all dense_high_card_low, with dense rating them very highly and the scorecard rating them comparatively low. R40 (rebutting a formal safety petition to NHTSA) shows the same pattern. A criterion naming the incident/conflict itself, independent of any brand language, would recover this signal.

proposals.name: Direct incident facts vs. reassurance-letter voice
proposals.instruction: Score whether a release describing a harm or crisis affecting third parties (customers, the public) states the hard facts of what happened -- scope, timeline, cause -- plainly and early, versus leading with apology, reassurance, and trust-affirming language that delays or dilutes those facts. A 10 = the incident's who/what/when/scope is stated plainly in the opening sentences, with reassurance language subordinate to it. A 0 = the release opens with and is dominated by apology/reassurance/trust language, with hard facts delayed, minimized, or given only in passing.
proposals.rationale: R02, R35, and R38 are the identical Target 2013 payment-card breach notice, written as a 'Dear Target Guest' letter that opens with brand-trust reassurance ('Our brand has been built on a 50-year foundation of trust...') before the scope of one of the largest retail breaches on record is stated. All three are dense_low_card_high: the scorecard rates this text quite high while dense rates it only moderately, suggesting dense is discounting the reassurance framing in a way the scorecard is not capturing as a distinct property.

proposals.name: Falsifiable claims vs. values self-congratulation
proposals.instruction: Score the ratio of concrete, falsifiable claims (numbers, named programs, specific dates, verifiable outcomes) to generic self-congratulatory language about values, culture, community, or mission that could appear in almost any company's release. A 10 = nearly every sentence carries a specific, checkable claim. A 0 = the release is dominated by abstract statements of values/mission/gratitude with few or no checkable specifics.
proposals.rationale: R13 (Salesforce's net-zero/'do well and do good' letter), R17 (Salesforce's IdeaExchange community-values post, which the scorecard rated at the absolute top of the pool, card_pct=1.000), and R31 (Target's CSR letter about 'five core beliefs') are all dense_low_card_high: the scorecard consistently over-credits generic mission/values prose relative to dense's assessment, even though little in these releases is a specific, checkable claim about a new event.

proposals.name: Textual integrity free of encoding corruption
proposals.instruction: Score whether the text is clean, correctly-encoded prose a journalist could quote directly, versus containing garbled characters, mis-decoded punctuation (e.g., a stray 'a' or 'aa' substituted for an apostrophe or dash), broken formatting, or other transcription corruption. A 10 = the text is fully clean and quotable with no encoding artifacts. A 0 = corrupted characters or broken punctuation appear repeatedly throughout, making direct quotation impossible without cleanup.
proposals.rationale: R13, R24, and R41 all contain repeated encoding corruption from mis-decoded smart quotes/dashes ('the worldas #1 CRM,' 'Iam proud,' 'weare not going to open up the doors'). All three are dense_low_card_high, i.e. the scorecard is not penalizing this corruption the way a human editor reading for publication-readiness would; a dedicated legibility criterion would let a judge flag this directly.

proposals.name: Independent celebrity, humor, or stunt hook
proposals.instruction: Score whether the release contains a hook that would draw journalistic interest on its own, independent of any business substance: a celebrity/public-figure tie-in, deliberate humor, a stunt, or a surprising human-interest angle. A 10 = a strong, self-contained novelty/celebrity/humor hook that could carry a story by itself. A 0 = no such hook, purely conventional business content.
proposals.rationale: R46 (Tesla's April Fools 'Model W' watch announcement) and R52 (Seth Rogen hosting an Airbnb stay tied to his Houseplant brand) are both dense_high_card_low: dense rates both fairly high while the scorecard rates both low, especially R52 (card_pct near the bottom of the whole slice). Neither item is 'newsworthy' in the hard-facts sense the scorecard likely rewards, but both carry an independent human-interest/novelty hook that a lifestyle or entertainment desk would plausibly cover.

proposals.name: Concrete named counterparty in a real arrangement
proposals.instruction: Score whether the release describes a specific arrangement (partnership, alliance, deal, collaboration) between the issuing organization and at least one other identifiable, independently-verifiable organization (by name and, ideally, ticker or registered entity), versus describing only internal initiatives or vague/unnamed partners. A 10 = a specific, named, independently-verifiable counterparty organization is central to a concrete described arrangement. A 0 = no named external counterparty is involved, or the 'partner' is vague or unspecified.
proposals.rationale: R08 (Target and Apple's in-store shopping partnership, with both companies' identities central to the announcement) and R32 (Cognizant, NASDAQ: CTSH, and Monitise, LSE: MONI, forming a named 'Mobile Money Alliance') are both dense_high_card_low. Dense rates both moderately-to-highly newsworthy -- two verifiable public companies doing something together is inherently reportable business news -- while the scorecard rates both low, R32 especially (card_pct near the very bottom of the slice).

proposals.name: Substantive vs. buzzword-filler attributed quotes
proposals.instruction: Score whether quotations attributed to named individuals convey new, specific information (a number, a mechanism, a concrete plan) rather than generic enthusiasm or buzzwords that could be deleted without losing information. A 10 = every attributed quote adds a distinct fact or specific claim not stated elsewhere in the text. A 0 = attributed quotes are interchangeable boilerplate/buzzword filler ('we're excited,' 'this is a huge shift') with no added information.
proposals.rationale: R32's executive quotes ('Mobile is, without question, the channel of the future') and R57's quote ('We're in the midst of an incredible technological shift...') are largely generic enthusiasm rather than new facts, yet both releases are dense_high_card_low -- dense still finds the underlying announcements (a named-company alliance; a new voice-assistant product launch) newsworthy despite the quote filler, while the scorecard rates both low. This suggests the scorecard may be conflating 'has attributed quotes' with quote substance, a distinction worth scoring separately.

proposals.name: Granular, locally verifiable operational specifics
proposals.instruction: Score whether the release supplies granular operational specifics -- named locations, store/site identifiers, exact dates, or counts -- precise enough that a local or trade reporter could act on them directly (e.g., confirm a nearby location or a specific rollout date), versus only vague aggregate or indefinite future-tense claims. A 10 = specific named locations/dates/counts are listed that a reporter could immediately verify or localize. A 0 = only vague, aggregate, or indefinite-future claims are given, with no locatable specifics.
proposals.rationale: R08 lists all 17 named Target stores getting the new Apple shop-in-shop, and R22 lists specific store counts, cities, and remodel-year targets for Target's expansion. Both are dense_high_card_low: dense rewards this granular, checkable operational detail, while the scorecard rates both releases toward the bottom of the pool, suggesting it does not specifically credit locatable, reporter-actionable specifics as distinct from general 'has numbers' density.

proposals.name: Self-sourced announcement vs. third-party analysis
proposals.instruction: Score whether the text is written as a first-person announcement by an identifiable organization about its own new action or decision, versus reading as neutral third-party market/industry analysis or news reporting that synthesizes others' data with no organization clearly announcing something about itself. A 10 = a clear organizational voice is announcing a new action it is taking. A 0 = the text reads as an analyst's or reporter's synthesis of market conditions or another party's events, with no releasing organization or first-person announcement present.
proposals.rationale: R03 (a Platts Analytics gas-to-oil switching market forecast), R23 (a multi-source news item about a UK airport passport-check lapse, quoting the UKBA, the airport, and Ryanair), and R56 (an S&P/Platts-style report on Winter Storm Elliott's grid outages) are all dense_low_card_high. None of the three has a clear organization announcing its own new action -- they read as finished, already-reported journalism or analyst synthesis -- yet the scorecard rates all three well above the median while dense rates them near the bottom, R23 at the very bottom of the entire slice.

proposals.name: Formal investor or regulatory procedural step
proposals.instruction: Score whether the release documents a formal step in a regulatory or investor process (an SEC filing, IPO registration, shareholder-meeting mechanics, proxy procedure) that would be independently reportable to financial/business press regardless of the surrounding narrative. A 10 = the release documents a specific, named regulatory/investor procedural step (e.g., a filing type, a meeting date, a registration) with enough detail to be reported as-is. A 0 = no such formal procedural step is present anywhere in the text.
proposals.rationale: R50 (Airbnb's confidential S-1 submission ahead of its IPO) and R11 (procedural details for Tesla's 2020 Annual Meeting and Battery Day, including how to obtain a control number to vote) are both dense_high_card_low. These are precisely the kind of formal corporate-governance/investor events that wire services and business press cover as a matter of course regardless of how dry the procedural language is, which dense appears to recognize and the scorecard does not.

proposals.name: Lead placement of the top newsworthy fact
proposals.instruction: Score whether the single most newsworthy fact in the release (the biggest number, the biggest change, the core event) appears within the first two or three sentences, versus being buried under throat-clearing, scene-setting, or procedural/administrative detail that a reader must wade through first. A 10 = the most newsworthy fact leads the release, stated in the opening sentences. A 0 = the most newsworthy fact, if present at all, appears only after substantial unrelated or procedural material.
proposals.rationale: R58 (Target's breach update plus a fourth-quarter earnings-guidance cut) opens with breach-investigation framing before burying specific EPS and margin figures under a wall of accounting detail, and R41 (Salesforce's office-reopening plan) opens with a paragraph of scene-setting ('I think this process will be like using a light dimmer, not a light switch') before any concrete plan detail. Both are dense_low_card_high -- the scorecard rates both quite high while dense discounts them -- consistent with the scorecard not penalizing a buried or diffuse lead the way dense implicitly does.

proposals.name: Breadth of external stakeholder impact
proposals.instruction: Score how many kinds of external stakeholders (competing companies, regulators, an entire industry, the general public/consumers at large) would need to act on or care about this release, versus it mattering only to a narrow, internal, or single-location audience (e.g., one office's employees, one community forum). A 10 = the content plausibly affects an entire industry, a regulatory landscape, or the general public. A 0 = the content is relevant only to a narrow internal group or a single, self-contained audience.
proposals.rationale: R15 (Tesla opening its charging-connector design to the entire auto industry as the 'North American Charging Standard,' directly affecting every competing automaker and charging network) is dense_high_card_low, with dense ranking it near the top of the pool and the scorecard near the bottom. By contrast, R51 (a single-office childcare center for Salesforce employees) and R29 (moving one Sydney conference online) are both dense_low_card_high -- narrow, single-audience content that the scorecard rates surprisingly high while dense correctly discounts it. The same axis explains both ends of the disagreement.

proposals.name: Discrete dated action vs. retrospective recap
proposals.instruction: Score whether the release centers on one discrete, dated action or change taking effect now ('starting today,' 'we have launched') versus being a retrospective summary, 'highlights' post, or celebratory recap of already-ongoing trends with no single new event at its core. A 10 = a single, clearly-dated new action is the unambiguous subject of the release. A 0 = the release is a recap/summary of pre-existing trends or past activity with no discrete new event.
proposals.rationale: R06 ('Starting today, all North American Model S Long Range Plus vehicles have an official EPA-rated range of 402 miles') and R57 ('today announced Einstein Voice') both center on one dated, unambiguous new action, and both are dense_high_card_low. R27 ('Celebrating our top new Hosts in each US state for 2022'), by contrast, is a retrospective, stat-filled recap with no single new event, and it is dense_low_card_high -- the scorecard rates it quite high despite there being no discrete news to report, while dense correctly rates it low.

proposals.name: Standard corporate boilerplate close
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much of this item's text is a fixed, formulaic company-description block (e.g., an 'About [Company]' paragraph, stock founding facts, or headquarters/founding-date recitation) rather than release-specific content. 0 = no such boilerplate block anywhere in the text; 10 = a large, clearly template-reused boilerplate block is present. Score only the EXTENT of boilerplate presence; do not judge whether the boilerplate itself is well-written, accurate, or appropriate to include.
proposals.rationale: R26 closes with a full 'About Cognizant' paragraph (headquarters, NASDAQ ticker, generic mission language) and R43 closes with an 'About Airbnb' paragraph (founding story, host/guest counts) that are structurally identical template inserts unrelated to that day's news; this is a drafting habit of the PR/comms process, not a marker of whether journalists would judge the item newsworthy.
proposals.upstream_parent: communications team's standardized template/house-style practice for closing out a release

proposals.name: Density of embedded numeric statistics
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how densely the text is packed with numeric figures (percentages, dollar amounts, counts, index values, dates-as-data) per sentence, independent of what those numbers refer to. 0 = almost no numbers anywhere; 10 = nearly every sentence contains at least one number/statistic. Score only the EXTENT of numeric density; do not judge whether the statistics cited are important, surprising, or credible.
proposals.rationale: R14 (S&P Case-Shiller home-price release) and R48 (Platts fuel-switching market report) are both saturated with percentages and volume figures sentence after sentence, yet one sits in dense_high_card_low and the other in dense_low_card_high -- this shows numeric density is a strong, direction-ambiguous textual fingerprint that a scorecard or a dense reader could latch onto regardless of the release's actual news merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: organization's routine practice of issuing data/index-driven reporting (recurring statistical release format)

proposals.name: Extraction-pipeline artifact text present
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much of the passage is NOT release prose but a visible remnant of an automated web-extraction or scraping process -- e.g., a trailing closing quote/brace, a code fence, or a meta-sentence stating what the page 'appears' or 'does not appear' to contain. 0 = no such artifacts, entirely release prose; 10 = the passage is dominated by extraction-process text rather than by any press-release content. Score only the EXTENT of visible pipeline artifact text; do not judge whether the release that was supposed to be captured (if any) would have been good.
proposals.rationale: R11 and R41 both end with a closing quote, a code-fence marker, and the sentence 'The provided raw page content does not appear to contain a press release...'; R44 carries the same pattern ('This page does not appear to contain a press release'). This is a pure artifact of how the item was mined/extracted and cannot reflect anything about how journalists would judge newsworthiness, since in these rows there may be little or no actual release content behind the artifact.
proposals.upstream_parent: the corpus's automated text-extraction/scraping pipeline that produced this row

proposals.name: Frames item as a reprinted communication
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the text explicitly frames itself as a copy or forward of a separate communication rather than being written directly as the release itself -- e.g., opening with 'The following email was just sent to...', 'Dear [Guest/Host],', or 'Below is an email ... sent to ...'. 0 = the text is written directly as the release, with no such framing; 10 = the entire item is explicitly presented as a reprinted/forwarded internal memo or letter. Score only the EXTENT of this framing device; do not judge whether the reprinted communication's content is important.
proposals.rationale: R01/R06 open with 'The following email was just sent to Tesla employees:'; R03/R05/R55 open with 'Dear Target Guest,'; R50 opens with 'Below is an email ... Brian Chesky sent to Airbnb hosts today.' This framing is a mining/format artifact, though it is 'mixed' because a leaked or reprinted internal executive email can also be genuinely more newsworthy than an ordinary release precisely because it is internal.
proposals.upstream_parent: the item was captured by the mining pool as a reprinted internal communication (email/letter) rather than as an originally-drafted press release

proposals.name: Named executive sign-off with title
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the text ends with, or is explicitly attributed throughout to, one specific named individual and their corporate title (e.g., 'Brian C. Cornell, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer'), as opposed to being issued anonymously in the company's institutional voice. 0 = no named individual signs or is credited; 10 = the piece is clearly signed/bylined by one specific senior named person with title stated. Score only the EXTENT of named personal sign-off; do not judge whether that person's seniority makes the content important.
proposals.rationale: R31 closes with 'Brian C. Cornell Chairman and Chief Executive Officer'; R34 is signed 'Cindy Robbins is EVP, Global Employee Success, at Salesforce.' A practiced senior signer may both be more likely to have their item favored by a text-perception model AND may genuinely produce more substantively newsworthy statements, so this is tagged mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: seniority and personal communications practice of the specific signing executive

proposals.name: Defensive rebuttal aimed at a named critic
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the text is structured as a direct rebuttal to one specific named external party (a news outlet, agency, or individual), using constructions such as 'X is fundamentally incorrect,' naming the accusing party repeatedly, and/or systematically listing and refuting specific claims attributed to them. 0 = no rebuttal structure, purely forward-looking announcement; 10 = the entire item is organized point-by-point around refuting a named external accuser. Score only the EXTENT of this rebuttal structure; do not judge whether the rebuttal is persuasive or factually correct.
proposals.rationale: R02 opens 'Fortune's article is fundamentally incorrect' and proceeds to refute it point by point; R24 systematically rebuts DFEH's discrimination allegations; R56 details Tesla's libel suit against 'Top Gear' with a bulleted list of specific misrepresentations. Being embroiled in a named, ongoing public dispute is plausibly also a genuine driver of real news value, so this is tagged mixed rather than a pure nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: an external dispute, media conflict, or litigation process that prompted this release to be issued reactively

proposals.name: Celebrity/public-figure brand tie-in language
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the release centers its narrative and quotes around one named, publicly-recognizable individual's personal brand/persona (as opposed to the corporate entity itself), including informal or colloquial phrasing distinctly associated with that individual's public image. 0 = no individual-brand framing, purely corporate voice; 10 = the release is built almost entirely around a named public figure's persona, quotes, and informal voice. Score only the EXTENT of this framing; do not judge whether the tie-in is appealing or effective.
proposals.rationale: R10 is built entirely around Seth Rogen's Houseplant persona, complete with colloquial phrasing ('Gloopy groupies and people who like nice things'); R01/R06 carry Elon Musk's distinctly informal, hyperbolic personal voice throughout an internal-email-framed announcement ('That is insanely badass'). A famous signer's large personal following is plausibly a nuisance driver of visibility that is separate from the underlying newsworthiness of the announced facts, though it can also coincide with genuinely more interesting content, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: the personal following/public profile of a named individual associated with the release, independent of the underlying corporate news

proposals.name: Presupposes an earlier installment in series
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the text uses language that presupposes the reader already knows about a prior, un-recapped announcement in an ongoing series on this topic -- e.g., 'update on,' 'is not a new X, but was uncovered as part of the ongoing...,' 'despite extensions on previous deadlines' -- versus language that introduces the organization and topic from scratch as if for a first-time reader. 0 = fully self-contained, introduces everything from scratch; 10 = the text heavily assumes reader knowledge of an earlier, un-recapped announcement. Score only the EXTENT of this presupposition; do not judge whether the update itself is significant.
proposals.rationale: R17 ('Target Provides Update on Data Breach... This theft is not a new breach, but was uncovered as part of the ongoing investigation') and R12 ('unable to reach a settlement... despite extensions on previous deadlines to negotiate a settlement') both assume the reader already tracks an earlier chapter of the story. Later installments of a fast-moving story can also be genuinely more newsworthy, so this is tagged mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the run of releases this organization has issued on this specific topic (a follow-up vs. an opening announcement)

proposals.name: Explicit first-of-kind or version marker
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the text explicitly foregrounds its ordinal position in a numbered or evolving sequence of the organization's own releases or products -- phrases like 'for the first time,' 'the first-ever,' 'Version 10.0,' or 'our biggest ever.' 0 = no such marker anywhere; 10 = the release explicitly and repeatedly foregrounds being first, latest, or a specific numbered iteration. Score only the EXTENT of this ordinal-position language; do not judge whether being first or latest actually makes the item more newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: R35 opens 'Introducing Software Version 10.0... our biggest software update ever' and R57 opens 'A first-ever analysis of Airbnb and OpenStreetMap data.' A genuinely first-of-kind milestone can be substantively more newsworthy on the merits, not merely stylistically flagged as such, so this is tagged mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: where this item falls in the organization's own communications timeline (an early/first-of-kind release vs. a routine repeat in an established program)

proposals.name: Formal wire-service dateline and ticker format
proposals.instruction: 0-10: rate how much the item opens with formal newswire conventions -- a capitalized CITY, STATE/COUNTRY dateline, an explicit wire-service name (e.g., 'PRNewswire'), and/or a stock ticker in parentheses (e.g., '(NYSE: CRM)') paired with an explicit 'today announced' construction -- versus an informal blog-post or social-caption opening with no dateline, wire branding, or ticker. 0 = none of these markers present; 10 = fully formatted like a paid-financial-newswire release with dateline, wire branding, and ticker. Score only the EXTENT of this formatting; do not judge whether the formal presentation makes the underlying news more important.
proposals.rationale: R26 explicitly opens 'TEANECK, N.J. and LONDON, Oct. 4, 2012 / PRNewswire /' and R40 opens 'SAN FRANCISCO -- Sept 20, 2018 -- Salesforce [NYSE: CRM] ... today announced,' both showing the full formal wire template, unlike the informal blog-style openings elsewhere in the slice (e.g., R09, R57). This is tagged mixed because SEC-regulated material announcements (mergers, offerings) are genuinely required to go out through this formal channel, so the format can coincide with real materiality as well as being a pure channel artifact.
proposals.upstream_parent: the distribution tier/channel the release was issued through (a major paid financial newswire vs. an organization's own owned blog/newsroom page)

proposals.name: Externally observable novelty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text describes a clearly new product, service, standard, or practice with a concrete mechanism; score 0 when it mainly restates existing activity or uses generic innovation language.
proposals.rationale: R08, R36, and R46 describe distinctly new offerings or technical arrangements, whereas many scorecard-favored items use broad claims without comparable novelty.

proposals.name: Scale of affected public
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the release quantifies a large affected population, infrastructure base, or geographic reach; score 0 when the subject is confined to a small internal group or narrow audience.
proposals.rationale: R02 concerns millions of electricity customers and major generating capacity, while R47 concerns up to 70 million people; R39 concerns only 116 children.

proposals.name: Immediate safety or harm stakes
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text presents concrete risks to life, physical safety, security, essential services, or major public welfare; score 0 when consequences are limited to convenience, branding, or lifestyle appeal.
proposals.rationale: R02, R18, and R30 describe power failures, physical assaults, and a border-security lapse; these stakes are largely absent from R39 and R54.

proposals.name: Named external conflict
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the release makes specific, consequential claims in a dispute with a named outside organization or person; score 0 when no identifiable adversarial relationship appears.
proposals.rationale: R13, R37, and R58 directly contest Fortune, a state agency, and Top Gear; this concrete conflict supplies a strong news hook that generic corporate updates lack.

proposals.name: Magnitude against a benchmark
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a claim is supported by a precise comparison with a prior period, rival, standard, or established benchmark; score 0 when magnitude is asserted through unsupported superlatives.
proposals.rationale: R14, R31, and R38 provide explicit index, time-series, or performance comparisons, while R52 relies on playful exaggeration rather than a substantive benchmark.

proposals.name: Cross-sector consequences
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text explains how the subject materially affects multiple industries, markets, institutions, or public systems; score 0 when benefits are limited to the issuing organization’s customers.
proposals.rationale: R17 and R20 connect battery materials and fuel switching to global energy and industrial markets; R06 connects mobile money to financial institutions and payment systems.

proposals.name: Regulatory or standards relevance
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the release directly concerns a regulator, court, public authority, legal framework, or industry standard and explains the practical implications; score 0 when no external rule-setting institution is involved.
proposals.rationale: R04 discusses tourism registration and local authorities, R26 concerns mine-safety litigation, and R46 addresses adoption by standards bodies.

proposals.name: Evidence transparency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the release identifies data sources, dates, methods, denominators, and relevant limitations; score 0 when important claims are unsupported or rely mainly on slogans and testimonials.
proposals.rationale: R14, R17, and R43 identify datasets, forecasts, surveys, or analytical methods; R10 and R29 make broad social claims with much thinner evidentiary detail.

proposals.name: Actionable immediacy
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text gives precise dates, locations, eligibility rules, access instructions, or affected boundaries that make the subject immediately usable; score 0 when timing and practical details remain vague or deferred.
proposals.rationale: R08 gives reservation timing and regional queues, R50 gives store dates and inventory limits, and R56 provides detailed event-access procedures.

proposals.name: Distinctive human-interest access
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the release offers unusual access to a recognizable person, remarkable place, or scarce experience with vivid concrete particulars; score 0 when it presents a routine product or corporate activity.
proposals.rationale: R51 combines Seth Rogen, a creative studio, and limited overnight stays; R01 uses unusual homes and visual settings, while R52 turns a product concept into an attention-grabbing joke.

proposals.name: Crisis-response accountability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text acknowledges a specific harm or failure, identifies affected parties, and gives concrete corrective or protective measures; score 0 when it offers only reassurance, values language, or generic monitoring.
proposals.rationale: R07 and R47 provide breach scope, customer protections, investigation details, and assistance; R59 gives a concrete response to a public-health disruption.

proposals.name: Social-practice shift
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the release documents a broad change in how people live, work, travel, or shop and connects it to measurable behavior or institutional adaptation; score 0 when it describes an ordinary internal initiative without wider behavioral significance.
proposals.rationale: R34, R48, and R49 describe remote work, dispersed tourism, and destination-level adaptation with population-scale indicators.

proposals.name: Operational commitment at scale
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text specifies substantial resources, coverage, staffing, rollout, or enforcement that make an initiative materially real; score 0 when it is primarily an aspiration, intention, or symbolic statement.
proposals.rationale: R15 specifies standards, enforcement channels, investment, and implementation timing; R32 specifies $200 million, 340,000 workers, and hundreds of programs; R35 details a multiyear store rollout.

proposals.name: Workplace-policy novelty and reach
