proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a new employment practice has unusual terms and affects a large workforce or a replicable model of work; score 0 when the subject is a routine benefit or a small workplace facility.
proposals.rationale: R34 describes location and compensation flexibility for Airbnb employees worldwide, and R32 covers debt-free education for more than 340,000 workers; R39 is a comparatively localized childcare facility.

proposals.name: External substance versus corporate puffery
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the release is dominated by verifiable external facts, public consequences, and specific mechanisms; score 0 when it is dominated by self-congratulation, values statements, or company-benefit language without an independent stake.
proposals.rationale: R02 and R47 foreground public consequences and checkable facts, while R10, R29, and R54 heavily emphasize corporate values, reputation, and general social-purpose claims.

proposals.name: Duplicated template blocks
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text repeats or near-repeats substantial blocks; do not judge whether the repetition is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Repeated key-takeaway and introductory blocks are visible in R01, R19, and R50. Such duplication can inflate length and token salience without changing the underlying event.
proposals.upstream_parent: editorial or CMS template practice

proposals.name: Broken character encoding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains visibly corrupted characters, missing punctuation, stray layout marks, or encoding substitutions; do not judge whether the text is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: R11 contains strings such as “emissionsafulfilling,” R12 contains repeated “A” artifacts, and R35 shows “Itas” and similar substitutions. These traces can affect textual processing while saying nothing about the event.
proposals.upstream_parent: copying, editing, or extraction pipeline

proposals.name: Syndication/agency package
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the item uses standardized wire-service or PR-agency packaging such as formal datelines, ticker symbols, release slugs, archive links, subscription prompts, executive quotes, and About sections; do not judge whether the package is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: R14 explicitly includes “PRNewswire,” while R04, R09, and R36 use highly standardized datelines, index-release language, URLs, and subscription prompts. These format traces reflect distribution workflow rather than the event itself.
proposals.upstream_parent: outside PR agency practice or paid distribution tier

proposals.name: Institutional scale signals
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text foregrounds organizational scale, reach, market leadership, employee or customer counts, global coverage, or infrastructure size; do not judge whether those claims are good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: R20 emphasizes 150,000 customers and ecosystem-wide economic effects, while R24 foregrounds 340,000 team members and R41 stresses five continents and over 40,000 offerings. Organizational scale can attract attention as a nuisance, while also plausibly contributing to genuine news impact.
proposals.upstream_parent: issuer size, prominence, and media relationships

proposals.name: Insider-email framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text uses direct internal-email framing, including greetings to employees or hosts, personal thanks, internal motivational language, or instructions to an in-group; do not judge whether the framing is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: R15 and R29 begin as emails sent to Tesla employees, and R57 reproduces an email addressed to Airbnb hosts. This audience-specific voice can change surface cues and verbosity without establishing independent news value.
proposals.upstream_parent: intended audience and author's practice in direct-email formats

proposals.name: Adversarial rebuttal language
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains denials, accusations, corrections, named opponents, legal threats, or defensive rebuttal wording; do not judge whether the conflict or wording is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: R13 rebuts safety allegations, R17 attacks a Fortune article, and R54 contests a government lawsuit. Conflict-heavy language can be disproportionately salient, although the underlying dispute may also genuinely affect newsworthiness.
proposals.upstream_parent: crisis-communications and rapid-response workflow

proposals.name: Page-shell extraction text
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the item consists of page-detection disclaimers, JSON fragments, product-page descriptions, navigation language, or statements that no press release was found; do not judge whether the page content is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: R28, R30, and R43 explicitly describe non-release pages or return extraction-shell text. This is a corpus-ingestion fingerprint that can strongly affect textual representation while carrying no intrinsic event value.
proposals.upstream_parent: receiving-side page selection and extraction process

proposals.name: Series-continuation wording
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text presupposes earlier installments through phrases such as “update,” “continued,” “as announced,” version numbers, prior initiatives, or retrospective references; do not judge whether the continuity is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: R01 repeatedly refers back to the 2020 party-ban announcement, R23 describes a continued safety program, and R25 announces Software Version 10.0. Such wording reveals stream position; first-versus-later position can also correlate with genuine novelty.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the organisation's entry stream

proposals.name: Calendar and embargo markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text exposes calendar or news-cycle conventions such as quarter-end references, holiday timing, conference schedules, exact event deadlines, embargo-style dates, or “for immediate release” wording; do not judge whether the timing is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: R15 refers to the final weeks of a quarter, R18 provides detailed meeting deadlines, and R48 is explicitly timed around Christmas shopping. These markers can affect reception and text style independently of the event's substance.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing and news-cycle conventions

proposals.name: Promotional audience address
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text uses direct consumer address, imperatives, sales language, booking instructions, discounts, lifestyle hype, or calls to mark calendars; do not judge whether the promotion is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: R27 uses playful booking language aimed at “Gloopy groupies,” R32 urges readers to shop scheduled deals, and R48 gives seasonal purchasing instructions. Promotional register can be highly machine-salient without indicating that independent journalists would value the item as news.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience/following and marketing-copy practice

proposals.name: Public consequence and reach
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the announcement describes a concrete change affecting public safety, security, infrastructure, livelihoods, or rights across a broad population; score 0 when effects are confined to routine internal or promotional matters.
proposals.rationale: R01 describes potentially safer transportation at scale, while R13 describes exposed payment data affecting millions of customers.

proposals.name: Breakthrough or first-of-kind claim
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the item clearly identifies a novel, unprecedented, first, fastest, longest, or category-defining development; score 0 when it describes a routine or familiar activity without a distinctive advance.
proposals.rationale: R21 claims unusually high vehicle performance and range, and R44 presents a proposed charging standard as a major industry-opening development.

proposals.name: Quantified comparative substance
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the release supplies several precise measurements, baselines, units, and comparisons that materially characterize the development; score 0 when it relies almost entirely on vague adjectives and unsupported generalities.
proposals.rationale: R17 and R59 provide detailed index movements against prior periods, while R06 uses exaggerated claims with almost no substantive measurement.

proposals.name: Credible external participation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when named regulators, governments, standards bodies, independent researchers, or outside institutions are directly involved or substantively cited; score 0 when the announcement speaks only through the issuing organization.
proposals.rationale: R03 names a state agency and its investigation, while R44 discusses standards bodies and external network operators.

proposals.name: Named conflict or accountability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text documents a specific dispute, allegation, investigation, lawsuit, or confrontation involving identifiable outside parties; score 0 when no opposing or accountable actor is present.
proposals.rationale: R03 contests allegations by a government agency, and R46 details a legal dispute with a major broadcaster.

proposals.name: Operational specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the item states exactly what will change, for whom, where, when, and how it will work; score 0 when it offers only broad intentions or slogans.
proposals.rationale: R12 specifies products, stores, rollout timing, and shopping mechanics, while R55 lays out concrete reopening procedures across locations.

proposals.name: Industry spillover potential
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the announcement could alter practices, compatibility, supply, or behavior across a wider ecosystem of firms or institutions; score 0 when its effects are limited to one organization’s ordinary operations.
proposals.rationale: R09 combines two firms around a platform for financial institutions, and R44 invites vehicle and charging companies to adopt a common connector.

proposals.name: Strong time-sensitive news peg
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the item is anchored to a clearly dated crisis, deadline, seasonal event, live market movement, or imminent launch; score 0 when its significance is essentially timeless.
proposals.rationale: R02 concerns a specific recent airport lapse, while R50 ties its analysis to rapidly changing energy prices and a defined forecast period.

proposals.name: Human-interest vividness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text contains an unusual person, recognizable public figure, dramatic incident, or vivid lived experience that gives the announcement an immediate human angle; score 0 when it is entirely impersonal and abstract.
proposals.rationale: R24 centers on a celebrity-hosted stay, and R38 recounts a vivid physical confrontation involving named journalists and security staff.

proposals.name: Immediate audience hook
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when readers can take a specific immediate action involving access, booking, purchase, attendance, or participation, especially under a clear deadline or limited availability; score 0 when no immediate audience action is presented.
proposals.rationale: R23 gives shoppers dated instructions for finding scarce toys, while R34 provides exact reservation channels and opening times.

proposals.name: Independent evidentiary support
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when claims are supported by named external datasets, studies, agencies, experts, or transparent methods; score 0 when claims are presented solely as company assertions without supporting attribution.
proposals.rationale: R29 cites federal data, an energy institute, grid operators, and quoted experts, while R49 identifies an IDC study and its survey base.

proposals.name: Crisis disclosure and remedy
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the item clearly identifies harm or exposure, specifies who may be affected, and describes concrete protective, compensatory, or investigative measures; score 0 when it offers only generic reassurance without particulars.
proposals.rationale: R13 details compromised information and protective services, while R53 explains cancellation policy changes, host payments, and relief funding during a crisis.

proposals.name: Material resource commitment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the announcement commits substantial money, staff, facilities, or geographic coverage to a defined initiative; score 0 when commitment consists only of values language or nonbinding aspirations.
proposals.rationale: R40 commits $200 million and education access for more than 340,000 workers, while R47 reports millions spent on pay-equity adjustments and related programs.

proposals.name: Self-contained announcement quality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text is a coherent, dated announcement with an identifiable subject, issuing organization, news peg, and complete supporting details; score 0 when it is merely a product page, listicle, fragment, or generic informational page.
proposals.rationale: R04, R22, and R43 explicitly lack identifiable press-release bodies, whereas R35 is a compact, clearly dated corporate announcement.

proposals.name: Caveated credibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the release openly states limitations, uncertainty, validation requirements, adverse facts, or qualifying conditions alongside its claims; score 0 when it relies on absolute superlatives, hype, or one-sided certainty.
proposals.rationale: R01 discloses calibration needs and temporarily unavailable features, while R21 includes testing qualifications and pricing limitations; R06 instead uses overtly exaggerated promotional language.

proposals.name: Direct-to-community address
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text addresses a bounded community as insiders, using labels such as hosts, guests, employees, or Trailblazers and direct invitations; score extent only, not whether this is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Audience-specific language can reflect an organisation's established community reach and communication habits, affecting uptake independently of journalistic value. Visible examples include the guest-facing guidance in R01, the host letter in R51, and the Trailblazer invitation in R60.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience/following

proposals.name: Executive email voice
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the item preserves an internal email or personal executive-letter voice, including first-person gratitude, emotional asides, informal claims, and direct address; score extent only, not writing quality or newsworthiness.
proposals.rationale: An author's habitual internal-communications style can leave a strong textual trace and influence circulation or attention without determining independent news value. The employee-email framing and informal praise are visible in R17 and R32, while R51 retains a CEO-to-host letter structure.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format

proposals.name: Reactive rebuttal framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text is framed as a response to criticism, allegations, litigation, regulators, or an opposing publication, using denials, corrections, adversarial references, or defensive chronology; score extent only, not whether the response is justified or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Reactive communications often arise during a heightened news cycle and may receive attention because of their timing, while the defensive framing itself is not a measure of journalistic importance. This fingerprint is prominent in R27, R33, R49, and R56.
proposals.upstream_parent: reactive submission timing

proposals.name: Series-template scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text displays recurring-series structure, such as duplicated key-takeaway blocks, predictable section headings, references to prior installments, or standardized update language; score extent only, not whether the template is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: A release's place in a recurring communications stream can produce serial language that is easy to recognize and process but does not establish independent news value. Repeated Key Takeaways and update-series cues appear in R13, R21, R23, and R25.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Publication-pipeline corruption
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the item contains visible extraction or publication artifacts, such as JSON residue, repeated replacement characters, malformed spacing, stray letters, broken markup, or explicit page-type disclaimers; score extent only, not whether the underlying material is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Pipeline failures can strongly affect how a text is parsed or classified while saying nothing about its journalistic value. JSON residue appears in R10, malformed characters and spacing in R14 and R26, and page-not-release disclaimers in R16 and R40.
proposals.upstream_parent: content ingestion or publication pipeline

proposals.name: Promotional call-to-action density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains consumer-promotion language, including discounts, booking or shopping instructions, urgency, product benefits, loyalty programmes, and invitations to visit a site or app; score extent only, not marketing effectiveness or newsworthiness.
proposals.rationale: Marketing-oriented drafting can attract attention through actionable consumer language independently of whether journalists would regard the announcement as news. Purchase and seasonal urgency dominate R01 and R31, while programme-benefit promotion is extensive in R54.
proposals.upstream_parent: in-house marketing practice

proposals.name: Recurring data-bulletin format
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the item follows a routine statistical bulletin format: fixed-period benchmark reporting, month-over-month or year-over-year comparisons, named indices, ranked geographies, source links, and subscription prompts; score extent only, not the importance or quality of the data.
proposals.rationale: A standardized analyst-bulletin format can be highly machine-recognizable and routinely distributed without its formatting being evidence of independent news value. The nearly identical Case-Shiller structures in R22, R30, and R58 provide clear fingerprints.
proposals.upstream_parent: recurring distribution or editorial desk practice

proposals.name: Calendar-and-embargo cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text foregrounds calendar or news-cycle markers, including exact event dates, quarter-end language, holidays, conference seasons, launch windows, embargo conventions, or 'for immediate release' phrasing; score extent only, not whether the timing is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Submission timing and calendar conventions can alter visibility and processing while leaving textual date cues that are unrelated to the release's intrinsic news value. Christmas-season language appears in R01, quarter-end language in R17, and event scheduling in R41 and R60.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing

proposals.name: Newswire/legal boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the item contains distribution or compliance boilerplate, such as wire-service labels, datelines, stock tickers, securities disclaimers, safe-harbor wording, formal offering language, or standard company descriptions; score extent only, not authority or newsworthiness.
proposals.rationale: Outside-agency and major-wire workflows leave recognizable legal and distribution traces that may affect reach or parser treatment without measuring journalistic value. PRNewswire and formal alliance boilerplate appear in R59, while securities-law language is explicit in R37.
proposals.upstream_parent: distribution tier or outside PR agency

proposals.name: Institutional credentialing density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text establishes issuer prominence through stock symbols, 'global leader' claims, executive titles, enormous scale figures, institutional affiliations, named analysts, or corporate superlatives; score extent only, not whether the organisation or claims are important or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: A prominent issuer's habitual credentialing and media-facing style can influence attention, while prominence may also correlate with genuinely newsworthy events, making this a sensitivity channel. Such markers are dense in R44 and R57, and also appear in the formal corporate framing of R22 and R59.
proposals.upstream_parent: issuer size, prominence, and media relationships

proposals.name: Hard original quantitative data
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release contains multiple specific, original numerical data points (percentages, price levels, index values, volumes, year-over-year comparisons) that are central to the story and that a journalist could lift directly into a news article. Score 0 if the release contains no quantitative data, or only vague round numbers used for decoration.
proposals.rationale: The dense model strongly rewards items built around citable data. R15, R16, and R29 (Case-Shiller index releases with specific city-level percentages and trends) and R38 (battery-recycling supply/demand tonnages and forecasts) all score dense_high. By contrast, R14 and R28 (Airbnb promotional pieces that sprinkle soft statistics into a marketing frame) score dense_low, suggesting the scorecard credits any number while the dense model looks for data that IS the story.

proposals.name: Named adversary and point-by-point dispute
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release explicitly names a specific critic, media outlet, regulator, or competitor and rebuts their claims point by point with evidence. Score 0 if no adversary is named or if disagreement is only implied generically.
proposals.rationale: Several of the highest dense_pct items are combative rebuttals: R10 (Tesla vs. a short-seller petition), R13 (Tesla vs. BBC/Top Gear), R18 (Tesla vs. Fortune), and R59 (Tesla vs. California DFEH). Journalists treat named, specifics-rich disputes as inherently newsworthy. The scorecard may reward the formal structure of a defensive statement without distinguishing whether a real adversary is being engaged.

proposals.name: Industry standard-setting or ecosystem-shaping action
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release announces an action that changes the rules, standards, or competitive structure for an entire industry (opening a proprietary standard, launching a cross-industry alliance, unilaterally redefining a market practice). Score 0 if the action affects only the issuing company's internal operations or product line.
proposals.rationale: R20 (Tesla opening NACS to all automakers) and R44 (Cognizant–Monitise mobile-money alliance) score dense_high because they reshape industry architecture. R19 (Airbnb UK tourism 'commitment' that merely voices support for existing government plans) and R36 (Airbnb voluntary guest standards) score dense_low—they describe company-internal policy dressed up as industry leadership.

proposals.name: Distinctive human voice, humor, or dramatic flair
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text carries an unmistakable individual personality—irreverent humor, emotional candor, vivid storytelling, or a distinctive first-person register that a journalist would want to quote. Score 0 if the prose is flat, committee-written corporate boilerplate with no quotable line.
proposals.rationale: R06 (Tesla April Fools' Model W announcement), R22/R50 (Elon Musk's internal employee email with phrases like 'insanely badass'), and R49 (a vivid, blow-by-blow account of a Gigafactory trespasser assault) all score dense_high. R08, R35, and R43 (well-structured but lifeless corporate prose) score dense_low, suggesting the scorecard rewards formal completeness while the dense model perceives the absence of a human voice.

proposals.name: Verifiable superlative or industry-first claim
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release makes a specific superlative claim ('fastest,' 'longest range,' 'first to exceed') that is concrete enough to be checked against known benchmarks. Score 0 if no superlative is made or if the claim is vague puffery ('best-in-class,' 'world-leading') that cannot be verified.
proposals.rationale: R32/R60 ('third fastest accelerating production car ever,' 'longest range production EV by far'), R21 ('official EPA-rated range of 402 miles'), and R26 ('all Tesla vehicles produced will have the hardware needed for full self-driving') all anchor dense_high scores on checkable superlatives. R07 and R28 (Airbnb pieces claiming leadership without a falsifiable benchmark) score dense_low.

proposals.name: Breadth of public or consumer impact
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the announced change directly and tangibly affects a large population of ordinary consumers or workers (millions of shoppers, all employees company-wide, entire user base). Score 0 if the audience affected is narrow (a single executive, a small community of enthusiasts, an internal team).
proposals.rationale: R03 (Target Deal Days sale reaching millions of shoppers), R52 (Airbnb's live/work-anywhere policy for all employees and guests), and R58 (debt-free degrees for 340,000 Target team members) score dense_high. R17 (a single C-suite appointment) and R35 (one on-site childcare center) score dense_low, suggesting the scorecard may credit formal significance while the dense model weighs how many real people are affected.

proposals.name: Serious dramatic incident with significant stakes
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release recounts a specific, time-and-place-bound dramatic incident involving physical danger, legal jeopardy, large-scale harm, or criminal conduct. Score 0 if no specific incident is described or if the incident is minor and inconsequential.
proposals.rationale: R49 (a Gigafactory trespasser running over a Tesla employee, resulting in felony arrests) and R09/R53 (a payment-card breach affecting tens of millions of customers) score dense_high. R54 (180 passengers walked through an airport without passport checks but no harm resulted) scores dense_low despite having an 'incident' frame—the dense model appears to weigh whether the stakes are genuinely significant.

proposals.name: Informational disclosure rather than self-promotion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release reads primarily as a factual disclosure or news report (neutral language, verifiable claims, minimal adjectival self-praise). Score 0 if the release is dominated by promotional language, self-congratulation, or brand marketing with little independent news value.
proposals.rationale: R15, R16, and R29 (S&P Case-Shiller index releases—dry, factual data dumps) and R38 (industry supply-chain analysis) score dense_high. R08 (Salesforce declaring itself a sustainability leader), R43 (Target CSR report self-narration), and R35 (Salesforce celebrating its own childcare center) score dense_low, suggesting the scorecard rewards the presence of positive content while the dense model discounts overt self-promotion.

proposals.name: Cultural crossover or named celebrity figure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release features a recognizable celebrity, public figure, or cultural institution (entertainer, major media programme, public official) that extends the story well beyond the usual corporate beat. Score 0 if all named individuals are company executives, analysts, or unknown private parties.
proposals.rationale: R46 (Seth Rogen hosting an Airbnb stay) and R13 (Tesla suing the BBC's Top Gear) score dense_high—both carry crossover appeal that would interest entertainment and culture desks, not just industry reporters. Almost all dense_low items (R08, R28, R35, R43) name only internal executives, limiting their reach.

proposals.name: Breaking-news timeliness and short shelf life
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release conveys time-critical information whose news value decays within days or weeks (a data release for a specific month, an IPO filing, a breach disclosure with an active window). Score 0 if the content is evergreen, could be published at any time, or describes an ongoing state rather than a time-stamped event.
proposals.rationale: R15, R16, and R29 (monthly Case-Shiller releases tied to a specific data month), R41 (Airbnb's confidential IPO filing), and R53 (Target breach update with a live enrollment window) score dense_high because journalists must act quickly. R19, R28, and R43 (Airbnb UK 'commitment,' host listicle, annual CSR essay) score dense_low—their content is not time-sensitive and could run any day.

proposals.name: Major structural or strategic pivot
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release announces a fundamental change in business model, corporate structure, capital markets posture, or labor policy that materially alters the company's trajectory (IPO, going public, universal work-from-anywhere, $200M education investment). Score 0 if the announcement is an incremental product tweak, a routine policy codification, or a phased operational plan.
proposals.rationale: R41 (Airbnb IPO filing), R52 (Airbnb live/work-anywhere redesign), and R58 (Target's $200M debt-free-degree program) score dense_high as structural pivots. R01 (codifying a temporary party ban as permanent) and R24 (a phased office-reopening matrix) score dense_low—the dense model perceives the difference between a genuine strategic shift and incremental operational continuity.

proposals.name: Format integrity: genuinely a press release
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the item is a coherent, self-contained press release with dateline, body text, and a clear news hook. Score 0 if the item is a product page, an error message, a scraped webpage fragment, or any other non-release content masquerading as one.
proposals.rationale: R23, R31, and R40 are explicitly identified in their own text as not being press releases (a sustainability page, a Model X product page, a Salesforce marketing page) yet all score dense_low_card_high—the scorecard appears to credit them despite their format failure, while the dense model recognizes they are not genuine releases and scores them near the bottom.

proposals.name: Insider-style transparency or internal revelation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release reveals content that is normally internal or private—employee emails, internal investigations, private incident reports, behind-the-scenes operational details—giving journalists access to material they would not otherwise see. Score 0 if everything described is already public or would be obvious from external observation.
proposals.rationale: R22/R50 (a verbatim internal Tesla employee email about record production and management changes) and R49 (a detailed internal security incident report) score dense_high because they offer a window into normally private corporate reality. R34 (Salesforce IdeaExchange community-management notes) and R24 (a generic office-reopening checklist) score dense_low—though internally focused, they lack the revelatory quality that makes insider content newsworthy.

proposals.name: Independence of the core data source
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the central findings rest on data or analysis from a genuinely independent third party (a government agency, a recognized index provider, an independent analyst firm cited on its own authority). Score 0 if the data is self-generated, self-commissioned, or produced by a partner paid by the issuer.
proposals.rationale: R15/R16/R29 (S&P Dow Jones Indices, an independent index provider) and R38 (S&P Global Market Intelligence analysts cited by name) score dense_high. R45 (an IDC study commissioned by Salesforce to promote Salesforce) and R14 (Airbnb analyzing its own platform data alongside OpenStreetMap) score dense_low—the dense model appears to discount research whose independence is compromised by commercial relationship to the issuer.

proposals.name: Concrete consumer-actionable product detail
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release provides enough specific detail (exact dates, prices, specs, reservation procedures, store locations, feature lists) that a consumer could take immediate, informed action. Score 0 if the release describes products, policies, or values only at a conceptual or brand level with no actionable specifics.
proposals.rationale: R21 (Model S range increase with specific engineering changes), R48 (Model 3 reservation process with dates, amounts, and regional queue logic), and R56 (Software V10.0 with a detailed feature-by-feature breakdown) score dense_high. R37 (Einstein Voice announced as a concept with no availability date or pricing) and R08 (Salesforce sustainability measures described abstractly) score dense_low, suggesting the scorecard may reward ambition while the dense model values actionable specificity.

proposals.name: Corporate blog conversational register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text uses informal, conversational, first-person-plural voice typical of a corporate blog post (casual phrasing, contractions, exclamation marks, humour, direct asides to the reader) rather than the formal third-person register of a wire-service press release. Do NOT judge whether the informal voice is good or bad; score only how much of it is present.
proposals.rationale: A distinctive blog voice is a practice/format fingerprint, not itself newsworthiness. Items like R09 ('Warning, current version requires wrist strength of an Orangutan') and R12/R50 ('That is insanely badass') and R10 ('Gloopy groupies') show heavy blog register that plausibly drives model scores apart without being what a journalist would judge as 'is this news.'
proposals.upstream_parent: organisation's communications practice (corporate blog vs. formal PR team)

proposals.name: Adversarial framing targeting named third parties
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text directly names, disputes, accuses or attacks a specific external party (a named publication, journalist, regulator, government agency, competitor or critic) in a defensive or combatorial manner. Count only instances where a named party is being confronted, not neutral references. Do NOT judge whether the confrontation is justified; score only how much adversarial framing is present.
proposals.rationale: Several dense-high items are organisational rebuttals—R05 ('brought by a Tesla short-seller'), R20 ('Fortune's article is fundamentally incorrect'), R30 (Tesla sues BBC Top Gear), R46 (DFEH lawsuit response). This adversarial posture is a communications-strategy fingerprint that may sway a model without being the same as whether the underlying event is newsworthy.
proposals.upstream_parent: organisation's adversarial media or legal strategy

proposals.name: Forwarded or republished internal communication markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text frames itself as a forwarded, re-posted or re-published message originally directed at an internal audience (employees, customers, community members) rather than at journalists — look for framing phrases like 'the following email was sent to,' 'below is an email,' 'the message below was posted,' or similar introductory wrapper language around what is clearly an internal memo or customer letter. Do NOT judge whether republishing was appropriate; score only how much of this framing is present.
proposals.rationale: R07/R22/R26 embed a customer letter with wrapper text ('The message below was posted from Target on Dec. 19, 2013'); R12/R50 open with 'The following email was just sent to Tesla employees'; R14 introduces 'Below is an email…sent to Airbnb hosts.' This wrapping is a distribution fingerprint, not a quality signal, yet it could strongly affect how a model scores the item.
proposals.upstream_parent: distribution practice of republishing internal communications as external content

proposals.name: Second-person non-journalist address density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text directly addresses a non-journalist reader using second-person pronouns and salutations ('Dear Guest,' 'Dear Host,' 'you can shop,' 'your trust,' 'we want you to know'). Count how much of the text is written as though speaking to a customer, employee or community member rather than to the press. Do NOT judge whether addressing the audience directly is good or bad; score only how much second-person address is present.
proposals.rationale: R07/R22/R26 ('Dear Target Guest…you can shop with confidence'), R14 ('Dear Host'), and R12/R50 (addressed to Tesla employees) are written to stakeholders, not to journalists. The choice of audience is an upstream production decision whose textual fingerprint—second-person address—may influence model scores independently of newsworthiness.
proposals.upstream_parent: item's primary intended audience (customers or employees vs. journalists)

proposals.name: Character encoding corruption
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text contains systematic character-level corruption — apostrophes and curly quotes rendered as stray letters (e.g., 'Itas' for 'It's', 'Weave' for 'We've', 'Iam' for 'I'm', 'Salesforceas' for 'Salesforce's') or other consistent glyph-substitution artefacts indicating an extraction or encoding pipeline problem. Do NOT judge whether the corruption makes the text hard to read; score only how much corrupted text is present.
proposals.rationale: R08 ('Itas a challenge that every CEO…', 'Weave completed the assessment'), R38 ('Iam helping develop Salesforceas plan'), and R51 ('Salesforceas most significant') show identical encoding artefacts. This fingerprint is purely a pipeline artifact with no plausible link to genuine newsworthiness, yet it could easily bias a text model.
proposals.upstream_parent: data extraction / scraping pipeline quality

proposals.name: Collection-error and non-release meta-content
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text contains meta-commentary, error messages, page-navigation residue or other indicators that the supplied text is NOT actually a press release body (e.g., statements like 'The provided raw page content does not appear to contain a press release,' code blocks, UI element text, or descriptive notes about a web page rather than the release itself). Do NOT judge whether the absence of a release is problematic; score only how much such meta-content is present.
proposals.rationale: R06, R55 and R57 all contain explanatory error text ('The provided raw page content does not appear to contain a press release…') rather than actual release content. These items have entered the pool through a collection error; their text is an artifact of the pipeline, not of the organisation's communications, yet models must still score them.
proposals.upstream_parent: collection / ingestion process error

proposals.name: Third-party newsroom attribution markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text contains markers that it was produced by a third-party news or analyst outlet rather than by the named organisation itself — look for phrases like 'according to [analyst/report],' named correspondents, wire-service byline formats ('Author / Theme / Metals'), references to being told something by a spokesperson, or analytical commentary about a company rather than by it. Do NOT judge whether the journalism is good; score only how much third-party newsroom attribution is visible.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('according to a March 9 report from the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis'), R04 (has 'Author / Theme / Metals' headers, cites analysts), R25 ('Airport International understands'), R45 ('according to estimates by Platts Analytics') and R56 all carry attribution fingerprints of third-party journalism. These items entered the pool despite not being press releases; a model's reaction to the journalism-style text is distinct from its reaction to genuinely newsworthy press releases.
proposals.upstream_parent: the item originates from a news or analyst outlet, not the named organisation

proposals.name: Self-promotional superlative intensity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text uses unqualified superlatives, superlative comparisons or self-congratulatory absolutes about the issuing organisation and its offerings (e.g., 'the global leader,' 'the most proven,' 'the perfect person,' 'no company has done more,' 'best paying jobs,' 'most amazing'). Do NOT judge whether the superlative claims are true or persuasive; score only how many are present.
proposals.rationale: R03 ('the global leader in CRM'), R02 ('the perfect person to lead this business'), R17 ('the most proven in North America'), R46 ('No company has done more for sustainability') and R52 ('Tesla's obsession with efficiency') are saturated with self-promotional absolutes. This marketing-register fingerprint could inflate or deflate model scores without tracking what makes a release newsworthy to a journalist.
proposals.upstream_parent: organisation's marketing / branding practice intensity

proposals.name: Recurring-series position presupposition
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text presupposes the reader's familiarity with an earlier item in a recurring programme or data series — look for formulaic 'today released the latest results' language, references to previous months' figures, 'as we announced in [date],' 'originally created in [year],' or other language that marks the item as one instalment in an established cadence rather than a standalone announcement. Do NOT judge whether being part of a series is good or bad; score only how much series-presupposing language is present.
proposals.rationale: R11, R21 and R31 are near-identical S&P Case-Shiller monthly data releases ('today released the latest results for the S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller Indices') with only the numbers changed; R49 presupposes 'In August 2020 we announced a temporary ban'; R27 references 'Originally created in 2006.' The fingerprint of being a routine serial instalment could bias models independently of whether any single instalment is newsworthy.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the organisation's recurring release stream (serial instalment vs. one-off)

proposals.name: Traditional wire-service structural formatting
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text follows traditional paid-wire press release structural conventions — a CITY/state dateline at the top, '/PRNewswire/ --' or similar wire tag, a 'today announced' lead sentence, a titled executive quote block, and a trailing 'About [Company]' boilerplate section. Count how many of these conventions are present. Do NOT judge whether traditional formatting is better; score only how much of it is present.
proposals.rationale: R19 ('TEANECK, N.J. and LONDON, Oct. 4, 2012 / PRNewswire / --'), R16 ('MINNEAPOLIS - January 10, 2014') and R47 ('MINNEAPOLIS - October 19, 2017') show full wire-service formatting with datelines, boilerplate 'About' sections and structured quotes. This formatting is a fingerprint of distribution tier and professional drafting — upstream factors that may correlate with both model scores and genuine newsworthiness without being the same thing.
proposals.upstream_parent: distribution tier and professional PR-agency drafting conventions

proposals.name: Novelty of core disclosure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release discloses genuinely new information never before made public—a first-ever product launch, a previously unknown event, a first-time data release. Score 0 if the release merely restates, summarizes, or repackages already-known information, or if it is a generic values statement with no specific news hook.
proposals.rationale: The dense model consistently elevates items that break news: R01 (first factory-wide self-driving hardware), R35 (first-ever IPO filing disclosure), R56 (first opening of charging standard). Meanwhile, the scorecard over-credits restatements and summaries: R04 (generic CSR recap), R59 (restating a 2015 net-zero commitment), R29/R41/R52 (not even press releases).

proposals.name: Specific verifiable quantitative claims
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release is dense with specific, independently verifiable numbers—technical specifications, prices, percentages, dates, mile ranges, dollar amounts—that a journalist could cite directly. Score 0 if the release contains almost no hard numbers or only vague qualitative claims ('significant,' 'industry-leading,' 'world-class').
proposals.rationale: High-dense items are packed with citable data: R01 (eight cameras, 250m range, 40x computing power), R09 (402-mile EPA range, 2% gains from specific components), R17/R33/R44 (exact Case-Shiller index percentages for named cities). Low-dense items like R04, R37, and R60 are almost entirely qualitative.

proposals.name: Conflict, controversy, or adversarial element
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release centers on an active dispute, lawsuit, public rebuttal, criminal incident, or dramatic confrontation with named opposing parties. Score 0 if there is no conflict, tension, or adversarial dynamic whatsoever.
proposals.rationale: The dense model strongly rewards controversy: R11 (Tesla vs DFEH lawsuit, dense 0.986), R19 (journalists arrested at Gigafactory, dense 0.850), R58 (Tesla suing Top Gear, dense 0.761), R45 (rebuttal of acceleration petition, dense 0.935). The scorecard may be penalizing adversarial tone as 'negative,' missing that journalists actively seek conflict-driven stories.

proposals.name: Market-moving economic data release
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release publishes original economic data, indices, or market statistics that are widely tracked by investors, policymakers, or analysts and could plausibly move prices or inform decisions. Score 0 if no original data is presented, or if the data is purely internal/company-specific with no broader market relevance.
proposals.rationale: R17 (dense 0.942), R33 (dense 0.915), and R44 (dense 0.932) are Case-Shiller home-price index releases—canonical market-moving data that every financial journalist covers. The scorecard rates them mid-range, likely because they read as dry. R05 (dense 0.495) similarly contains commodity supply-chain data with real market relevance.

proposals.name: Superlative or record claim with evidence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release makes a specific superlative claim (first, fastest, largest, longest, only) AND provides concrete evidence backing it (test methodology, named benchmark, comparison data). Score 0 if no superlative is claimed, or if superlatives are asserted without any supporting evidence.
proposals.rationale: R24/R49 ('third fastest accelerating production car ever,' with 0-60 time and LaFerrari/Porsche 918 comparison) exemplify this: dense rewards the specific record claim with evidence. R09 ('longest-range production EV' at 402 EPA miles) and R56 ('most proven charging connector' with 20 billion miles data) follow the same pattern. Items like R04 and R60 make vague superiority claims with no evidence.

proposals.name: Named competitor or explicit comparative benchmark
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release explicitly names competitors (companies, products, or technologies) and positions the issuer's offering against them with specific comparisons. Score 0 if no competitor or external benchmark is mentioned anywhere in the text.
proposals.rationale: R24/R49 name LaFerrari and Porsche 918 Spyder with price and seat-count contrasts. R56 names CCS as the competing standard with quantitative comparison. R02 humorously references 'some other company.' This explicit positioning signals news value because it stakes a claim journalists can investigate. Low-dense items like R03, R39, and R55 never mention a competitor.

proposals.name: Concrete actionability for consumers or users
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release tells the audience something they can immediately act on—buy a product today, make a reservation, apply for a benefit, use a new feature, access a service—with specific dates, prices, or URLs. Score 0 if the release describes something abstract, internal, or future with no way for the reader to act.
proposals.rationale: R01 (customers can buy today), R46 (Model 3 reservations opening March 31 with exact time and link), R38 (Target Deal Days with exact dates and shopping methods), R57 (book Seth Rogen stay at specific URL and price). These create immediate reader action. Contrast R37 (internal IdeaExchange redesign) or R55 (office reopening principles) where the reader can do nothing.

proposals.name: Factual density relative to length
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if nearly every sentence contains a discrete, citable fact, statistic, name, date, or specific claim—the text is 'all signal, no noise.' Score 0 if the text is dominated by boilerplate mission statements, generic value propositions, or repetitive restatements of the same idea with few embedded facts.
proposals.rationale: R17, R33, and R44 pack each sentence with index values, city names, and percentage changes. R09 lists specific engineering changes (Tempest wheels, electric oil pump, HOLD mode). In contrast, R04 (dense 0.283) and R60 (dense 0.109) are almost entirely corporate platitudes with minimal factual content per paragraph.

proposals.name: Named external authority or independent sourcing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release cites multiple named, independent external sources—government agencies, regulators, academic researchers, named industry analysts, third-party data providers—whose statements or data are central to the story. Score 0 if all claims are self-sourced with no external validation.
proposals.rationale: R05 cites S&P Global Market Intelligence data, the IEA, Alice Yu (named analyst), Ajay Kochhar (CEO of Li-Cycle), Adrian Griffin (Lithium Australia), and government agencies—dense rewards the multi-source richness. R11 references DFEH, NHTSA, and the court system. R17/R33/R44 cite the S&P DJI methodology. Low-dense items like R37, R39, and R59 are entirely self-referential.

proposals.name: Cross-industry or ecosystem-wide implications
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the announcement has direct consequences for multiple companies, entire industries, supply chains, or regulatory regimes—not just the issuing organization. Score 0 if the implications are confined entirely to the issuer's internal operations with no spillover effects.
proposals.rationale: R56 (opening the charging standard to all automakers and networks) reshapes an entire industry's infrastructure. R01 (all Teslas get self-driving hardware) affects autonomous driving broadly. R05 (battery recycling supply gap) touches EV makers, miners, and recyclers globally. Low-dense items like R37 (IdeaExchange redesign) and R60 (one childcare center) affect essentially nobody outside the company.

proposals.name: Absence of self-congratulatory or promotional framing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release reads like straight factual reporting—no phrases like 'we are thrilled,' 'proud to announce,' 'industry-leading,' 'unprecedented,' or other marketing language. Score 0 if the text is saturated with promotional adjectives, congratulatory self-assessment, and emotional appeals.
proposals.rationale: R17/R33/R44 (Case-Shiller releases) are nearly pure data with zero promotional language—and the dense model strongly rewards them. R11 and R45, while opinionated, are written as factual rebuttals, not marketing. Conversely, R03 ('equality is a core value'), R04 ('really proud'), R59 ('proud to share'), and R60 ('thrilled to announce') are dense with promotional framing that journalists often discount.

proposals.name: Human drama or narrative tension
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release contains a compelling human story—a dramatic incident, personal stakes, vivid narrative detail, or emotional tension that would draw a reader in. Score 0 if the release is entirely impersonal with no human narrative element.
proposals.rationale: R19 (journalists hitting a Tesla employee with their Jeep, with specific injury descriptions) is pure narrative drama—dense 0.850. R10 (Airbnb CEO apologizing to hosts during COVID, $250M fund) has genuine emotional stakes. R58 (Tesla suing Top Gear over staged breakdowns) reads as a dramatic showdown. The scorecard may not credit narrative tension as newsworthy.

proposals.name: Recognizable public figure or celebrity involvement
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release features a widely recognizable public figure, celebrity, or named individual (beyond corporate executives in their official capacity) whose involvement is central to the story and broadens its audience beyond the industry beat. Score 0 if no public figure or celebrity is involved.
proposals.rationale: R57 (Seth Rogen hosting an Airbnb stay, dense 0.631) gets elevated by the dense model because celebrity involvement generates broader coverage. R02's April Fools' tone (dense 0.686) similarly creates viral potential. R21/R34 name Jerome Guillen's Daimler pedigree, but the real driver is Elon Musk's voice permeating the text. Low-dense items feature no recognizable external figures.

proposals.name: Scale of population or market directly affected
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the announcement directly affects a very large population—millions of consumers, a national market, an entire workforce—or a very large geographic area. Score 0 if the affected population is tiny (a single office, one department, a handful of people).
proposals.rationale: R23 (340,000 Target employees get debt-free degrees, $200M investment) affects a massive population—dense rewards it at 0.488 vs card 0.147. R01 (all Tesla vehicles globally) and R56 (entire North American EV market) have vast scale. R60 (childcare center for 116 children at one office) and R55 (reopening guidelines for internal offices) affect tiny populations that journalists would not prioritize.

proposals.name: Competitive landscape shift together with concrete mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release describes a concrete mechanism (partnership, standard-setting, pricing change, new market entry) that materially alters the competitive structure of an industry, AND specifies how the shift will work in practice. Score 0 if no competitive shift is described, or if one is only vaguely asserted without mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R56 (opening NACS to all automakers with downloadable specs and standards-body engagement) is a textbook competitive landscape shift with concrete mechanism—dense 0.857. R28 (Target-Apple partnership with 17 named store locations) shifts the retail electronics landscape with specifics. R35 (Airbnb IPO filing) reshapes the competitive landscape for travel platforms. Contrast R13 (vague support for UK regulation) and R31 (listing 20 destinations with no mechanism) which assert relevance without concrete competitive shift.

proposals.name: Extraction Artifacts & Markup
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text contains raw web page markup, JSON code blocks, or explicit meta-commentary indicating the text is an extracted web page rather than a clean press release (e.g., 'This page does not appear to contain...', repetitive headers, code brackets). Do not judge the quality of the release, only the presence of these textual artifacts.
proposals.rationale: R10, R15, and R60 contain literal JSON payloads and extraction failure messages. These are systemic quirks of the corpus collection that can heavily skew a text-only model's perception, but are orthogonal to actual newsworthiness.
proposals.upstream_parent: system data collection error

proposals.name: Proprietary Internal Lexicon
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text relies on proprietary internal terminology, community branding, or forced corporate jargon (e.g., 'Ohana', 'Trailblazer', 'Bullseye View'). Do not judge whether the use of this language is good or bad, only how frequently and prominently it appears.
proposals.rationale: Releases like R01, R07, R20, and R40 use heavy community branding (Salesforce's 'Ohana', Target's 'guests'). This stylistic choice reflects company culture and internal PR practices, which might influence scorecards but is not an indicator of newsworthiness.
proposals.upstream_parent: corporate culture and internal PR practice

proposals.name: Verbatim Text Duplication
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text contains verbatim duplicated blocks of text, such as repeating the same 'Key Takeaways' bullet points or copying a previous corporate statement verbatim within the same release. Do not judge the quality of the writing, only the presence of repeated text.
proposals.rationale: R26 and R46 literally duplicate their 'Key Takeaways' bullet points verbatim immediately after stating them, while R12, R28, and R39 contain verbatim nested reprints of older messages. This is an editorial or templating artifact that a model might penalize or reward spuriously.
proposals.upstream_parent: content management system template dynamics

proposals.name: Epistolary Direct Address Format
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text is formatted as a direct letter or email to a specific audience (e.g., using salutations like 'Dear Target Guest', 'Dear Host', or framing as 'The following email was just sent to Tesla employees'). Do not judge the effectiveness of the format, only its presence.
proposals.rationale: R05, R12, R25, and R28 adopt an epistolary format. This upstream choice—drafting a letter to stakeholders instead of a traditional press release—alters the text's structure and tone, affecting how models score it without inherently determining its journalistic value.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience communication strategy

proposals.name: Adversarial & Defensive Posture
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text adopts a defensive posture, directly refutes specific external claims, criticizes named journalists or outlets, or argues against regulatory actions. Do not judge the validity of the defense, only the extent of its adversarial nature.
proposals.rationale: R18, R22, R45, and R54 aggressively rebut media reports or regulators (e.g., Fortune, Top Gear, DFEH). Crisis communication fingerprinting strongly influences text-only models' perception of tone, but defensiveness is an upstream reaction to external events, not an intrinsic measure of news value.
proposals.upstream_parent: crisis communications and legal response

proposals.name: Consumer Marketing Call-to-Action
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text reads like a retail advertisement or product launch aimed at consumers, featuring pricing instructions, shopping deadlines, event booking links, or promotional slogans. Do not judge the quality of the marketing, only the presence of consumer calls-to-action.
proposals.rationale: R23, R33, R37, and R49 feature product placements and retail promotions (e.g., Hatchimal hunts, Target Deal Days). This upstream factor—drafting by a product marketing team rather than corporate communications—leaves clear textual calls-to-action that scorecards might misinterpret as substantive detail.
proposals.upstream_parent: product marketing practice

proposals.name: Quantitative Data & Index Dump
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text consists primarily of dense numerical data, percentages, specific financial metrics, and index values with minimal narrative context. Do not judge the accuracy or importance of the data, only the density of the quantitative dump.
proposals.rationale: R34, R36, R44, and R47 are heavy data dumps. The upstream factor is SEC or industry reporting requirements. Dense numerical text can skew scorecard evaluations for 'comprehensiveness' while dense models might perceive it as boilerplate, neither of which strictly maps to newsworthiness.
proposals.upstream_parent: compliance and reporting requirements

proposals.name: Serial Routine Update Language
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text explicitly presupposes prior knowledge of an ongoing program or updates a recurring metric (e.g., 'As you have likely heard by now', 'In August 2020 we announced... today we are codifying', referring to prior months' indices). Do not judge if the update is good, only the extent to which it relies on its position in an ongoing series.
proposals.rationale: R12, R28, and R39 are identical updates on the same data breach. R26 codifies an earlier temporary ban. R36, R44, R47 are nth-in-series monthly index reports. Position in the stream leaves a clear textual fingerprint of presupposing prior context, which can confuse text-only models evaluating standalone newsworthiness.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Formal Newswire vs Blog Structure
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text features traditional paid newswire formatting (e.g., datelines like 'MINNEAPOLIS - January 10, 2014', 'PRNewswire') versus an informal corporate blog format lacking a dateline but featuring 'By [Author]' tags. Do not judge the quality of the format, only its strict adherence to formal newswire layout.
proposals.rationale: R52 and R57 exhibit strict traditional newswire formatting, whereas R07, R59, and R16 read like casual corporate blog posts. This upstream prior (distribution tier: paid newswire vs. own newsroom) leaves strong formatting fingerprints that scorecards often explicitly reward, despite format not equating to newsworthiness.
proposals.upstream_parent: distribution tier and PR agency practice

proposals.name: Third-Party Analyst & Data Citations
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text features quotes or citations from external third parties, named analysts, or specific research firms (e.g., 'IDC forecasts', 'Platts Analytics estimated', 'according to...'). Do not judge the credibility of the third party, only the frequency of external citations.
proposals.rationale: R27, R34, and R53 lean heavily on analyst quotes and third-party data (IDC, S&P, Platts). PR agencies often insert these to add perceived weight. While this might impress a scorecard model looking for 'evidence,' the mere presence of analyst quotes is an upstream drafting technique, not an inherent measure of newsworthiness.
proposals.upstream_parent: media relationships and PR agency drafting
